title: Installation and running
text: This page covers building VILMA2, testing the build, and running a forced simulation. The build is driven by configme (one source of machine and compiler settings) and runs are staged by runme (single simulations and ensembles, locally or on SLURM). The model is built and tested on three machines: a MacBook (gfortran), the AWI cluster albedo (ifx) and the DKRZ cluster levante (ifx). Production runs are currently made on albedo.

The fesm-utils branch is pinned in .configme/manifest.toml, so a checkout records the ref it needs. title: Installation and running
text:
Install
configme install vilma2 clones fesm-utils into the checkout, builds its serial and OpenMP variants (FFTW, SHTns, LIS and libfesmutils; about 10 minutes), and writes the top-level Makefile from config/Makefile and the machine and compiler fragments. configme show <machine> prints a fragment, configme status reports what is present and what is pending, and configme config vilma2 regenerates the Makefile of an existing checkout without cloning. To reuse an existing fesm-utils checkout instead of cloning one, add --link fesm-utils=/abs/path/to/fesm-utils.
The optimization flags differ by machine. The macbook fragment is the repository’s own (.configme/machines/macbook.mk): gfortran -O3 -mcpu=native -funroll-loops -ffast-math. The clusters use configme’s fragments: ifx -Ofast -march=znver2 -traceback on albedo (AMD EPYC 7702) and -Ofast -march=znver3 -traceback on levante (AMD EPYC 7763). The benchmark numbers in these pages were measured with the albedo build.

MacBook (gfortran)
brew install gcc netcdf netcdf-fortran
pip install git+https://github.com/fesmc/configme.git git+https://github.com/fesmc/runme.git
git clone git@github.com:fesmc/vilma2.git && cd vilma2
configme install vilma2 -m macbook -c gfortran
make -j 8 vilma
make check


AWI albedo (ifx)
The system git has been removed from the login nodes, so load the git module first. The Intel compiler and netCDF modules must be loaded before configme runs, so that it finds nf-config.
module load git intel-oneapi-compilers netcdf-c netcdf-fortran
git clone git@github.com:fesmc/vilma2.git && cd vilma2
configme install vilma2 -m awi_albedo -c ifx
make openmp=1 -j 8 vilma            # on the login node, at most -j 8
Compile on the login node and run the tests and the model through SLURM (see Testing the build). The compute nodes have no git. The build does not need it: the version string compiled into the model comes from git describe and falls back to "unknown" where git is missing.


DKRZ levante (ifx)
module load git intel-oneapi-compilers netcdf-c netcdf-fortran
git clone git@github.com:fesmc/vilma2.git && cd vilma2
configme install vilma2 -m dkrz_levante -c ifx
make openmp=1 -j 8 vilma
The build on levante has been verified (ifx 2023.2, netCDF-Fortran 4.6.2). No runs have been made there yet.

title: Installation and running
text:
Build
make vilma        # -> bin/vilma.x        (standalone forced-run driver)
make vilma_mkref  # -> bin/vilma_mkref.x  (build a Gauss-grid reference state)
make vilma_remap  # -> bin/vilma_remap.x  (offline lon-lat -> Gauss remap)
make vilma-static # -> libvilma/include/libvilma.a and the .mod files
make bench_visc3d # -> bin/bench_visc3d.x (lateral-viscosity benchmark driver)
make vilma-static is the library that a host (kryos, CLIMBER-X) links: objects, .mod files and libvilma.a are written to libvilma/include/, and the archive is rebuilt only when an object changes. openmp=0 and openmp=1 share that directory. Changing the setting rebuilds every object, and the host must use the matching fesm-utils variant (include-serial or include-omp).
Build switches: debug = 0|1|2 (optimized, checks, profile), openmp = 0|1 (default 1) and vilma_v1 = 0|1 (the optional VILMA1 backend, see doc/vilma-v1-backend.md). The threaded degree loop is what makes production resolutions fast (see Solver). After switching to another fesm-utils checkout, run make clean: objects compiled against the old module files can fail to rebuild.

title: Installation and running
text:
Testing the build
make check                  # the test suite: about 50 tests, ~2 min
make openmp=1 check-slow    # full-resolution benchmarks and order tests, ~10 min on 32 threads
Both targets run every test, print a summary that names the failing tests, and exit with a non-zero status if any failed. check-slow runs the four sea-level benchmark cases, the low-viscosity-zone benchmark, the off-pole rotational-invariance test at \(\ell_\max = 128\) and three convergence-order tests (strain–memory coupling, sea-level–memory coupling, adaptive step control). It raises the stack limit itself. Setting VILMA_BENCH_DUMP to a directory makes the benchmark tests write their comparison tables there (see Benchmarks).
On albedo, run both suites in a job, with the executables built beforehand on the login node (make openmp=1 -j 8 check builds them and then runs the tests; interrupt it once the build is done, or build the targets listed in TESTS and SLOW in config/Makefile_vilma.mk). A minimal job script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<project> --partition=smp --qos=12h --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32 --mem=60G
source ~/.bash_profile
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
make openmp=1 check; make openmp=1 check-slow
Known state. With ifx -Ofast on albedo, all 49 tests of make check and all 9 runs of make check-slow pass, with the default stack settings. A GitHub workflow builds the model with gfortran on Ubuntu and runs make check on every push and pull request to main.

title: Installation and running
text:
Configuration: &vilma and &ctl
A run configuration has two namelist groups:

&vilma: the model’s physics and numerics. This is the record a host model fills in memory.
&ctl: the standalone run itself: forcing, reference and output files, the time window, i_eq, online remapping and the restart path. A host model never reads it.

The complete, documented &vilma defaults are in input/vilma_defaults.nml and are loaded automatically. A run configuration such as vilma.nml (the default) or examples/deglac_lgm.nml carries the full &ctl group plus only the &vilma parameters it overrides (the yelmo defaults_file convention). A &vilma key the defaults file does not declare, such as a typo or a renamed parameter, stops the run:
./bin/vilma.x examples/deglac_lgm.nml    # default: vilma.nml
./bin/vilma.x run.nml my_defaults.nml    # optional second argument: another defaults file
vilma_remap.x and vilma_mkref.x take the same optional second argument; they too need the full &ctl group.
A few conventions worth knowing:

Time fields (dt_*, time_*, equil_time_max) are given in years in the namelist and converted to SI seconds on load; equil_rate_tol is in m/yr. Everything else is SI. A host that fills se%par in memory sets the time fields in seconds.
Earth structure is chosen by earth: a named built-in ("M3-L70-V01", or "PREM", which fills \(\rho,\mu\) from shell averages of incompressible PREM on the given layer geometry) or "custom" to assemble from the surface-first layer arrays. The radial mesh follows the depth of each element (see Radial finite elements).
Response solver is chosen by earth_response: "ve" (full viscoelastic, default), "elastic", or "null".
Memory scheme is chosen by scheme: "fe" (explicit, default) or "trap" (2nd-order, adaptive); see Rheology.
Degree-1 frame is chosen by deg1_frame: "cm" (default) or "cf"; see Sea-level equation.
Reference state is chosen by i_eq (&ctl). Relative sea level is measured against this relaxed reference.

0: the state at the start of the run window is the equilibrium: the forcing’s ice at that slice and the bed name_z_bed_start, read from file_forcing (lon, lat, time) or, with remap_input = .false., from the 2-D file_ref.
1 (default): a present-day reference from z_bed_ref_file and h_ice_ref_file, so that rsl is about zero at the present day.
2: an equilibrium state read from z_bed_eq_file and h_ice_eq_file (e.g. an LGM state).
3: the present-day reference bed plus the rsl field of rsl_restart_file.

The variable names in these files are set by name_z_bed_ref, name_h_ice_ref and name_rsl.
Spin-up is controlled by equil_time_max, equil_rate_tol (the memory is relaxed under the start-of-run load until the bed is stationary) and pre_spinup_1d (a cheap 1-D pre-equilibration first); see Spin-up.
3-D viscosity is enabled with l_visc_3d = .true. and a lateral log10(eta) field (visc_3d_file). With visc_3d_structure = n (n ≥ 1) the file is in the FesmData layout (log10_visc on lon, lat, depth, structure) and structure n is read. The default is the FesmData product fesmdata/Global/GLOBAL-T170/GLOBAL-T170_SolidEarth-Bagge2021.nc (Bagge et al. (2021); structure 6, v_1.0_s16). The path is relative to the run folder, which needs a fesmdata link to the FesmData store (on levante /work/ba1442/fesmdata). The model does not ship a viscosity file. The field can be shifted by f_visc_sd standard deviations (σ from the variable name_visc_sd, or f_visc_rel |log10 η|) and by region and depth with visc_shift_file. It is then clamped to visc_log10_min–visc_log10_max, and visc_3d_lid_depth and visc_3d_lid_log10max make its top effectively elastic. visc_3d_tol sets which elements are treated as genuinely 3-D. The order of these steps is given in Rheology.
Toroidal flow (l_toroidal) is on by default: with lateral viscosity it changes local relative sea level near former ice sheets by up to about 90 m in a deglaciation, though global means only by centimetres. l_toroidal = .false. makes such runs 1.5–1.8 times faster, for quick runs that do not depend on local sea level (see Toroidal flow).
Rotational feedback (l_rotation) is on by default for real-Earth runs. Set l_rotation = .false. for the non-rotating community benchmarks. The secular Love number in the Liouville equation defaults to the model’s own fluid limit; rotation_k_s (> 0) prescribes it and rotation_c_minus_a sets C − A (default 2.63e35 kg m²).
Forcing. The ice-thickness forcing is a lon-lat field (global or regional) on a time axis in years (kyr is converted; ages and other units stop the run) that must be strictly ascending. The ice ramps linearly between slices. The axes name_lon, name_lat are cell centres; longitudes must ascend, latitudes may ascend or descend. A regional source is remapped with its mass conserved and no ice outside it. Missing, non-finite or out-of-range values stop the run (put zero where there is no ice). The remap weights are cached in maps/ in the working directory, keyed by the grid dimensions and a hash of the axis values.
Output. file_out receives the diagnostic surface fields at every forcing slice, including the convergence of the sea-level solve (sle_resid, the worst relative inner residual of the interval, and sle_n_cap, the number of solves that ended at an iteration cap; the model also warns once per interval when a cap is hit). The folder of file_out is created if needed. file_hor (optional) receives the horizontal surface displacement. The variables and their output precision are listed in input/vilma-variables.md. Diagnostics are rounded to that precision. write_lossless = .true. (&ctl) writes them lossless, as needed for bit-for-bit comparisons. Restart files are always lossless.
Restart. The driver writes the full model state to spinup/vilma_restart.nc after the spin-up and to final/vilma_restart.nc at the end of the run, in the run directory. restart_in_file (&ctl) resumes from such a file: the model is initialized at the reference and the saved state is restored, so a resumed run continues the original one bit for bit. If a spin-up is enabled, it then runs from the restored state. A restart from a lower degree is padded: its memory fills the shared low degrees and the higher degrees start at zero (not bit for bit). The run resumes at the restart’s time: a time_init that selects another start stops it, unless restart_time_reset = .true. (&ctl), which takes the restart as the state at the start of the window. A restart from another radial mesh is refused. A restart from another viscosity (radial profile or 3-D field, both stamped in the file) is refused unless restart_other_visc = .true. (&ctl), which uses its memory as a seed. Restarts of the default PREM model written before the depth-based mesh rule (220 instead of 219 elements) are therefore refused; mesh_depth = 80e3, 670e3 rebuilds the old mesh exactly. What the restart carries and what is checked on read is described in Time stepping.
Backend is chosen by solver: "v2" (this model, default) or "v1", the VILMA1 library behind the same driver, forcing and output for like-for-like comparison (requires a build with vilma_v1=1).

title: Installation and running
text:
The drivers







Executable
Role




bin/vilma.x
reads a reference state and an ice-thickness forcing h_ice(lon,lat,time), marches the model across the forcing (online lon-lat → Gauss remap by default), and writes the diagnostic surface fields (rsl, z_bed, h_ice, ocean function) to file_out, and optionally the horizontal surface displacement to file_hor


bin/vilma_mkref.x
generates the canonical Gauss-grid present-day reference (e.g. RTopo) used by i_eq = 1; other resolutions remap it online (cached in maps/)


bin/vilma_remap.x
offline conservative lon-lat → Gauss remap, to preprocess a forcing onto the model grid (remap_input = .false.)



A complete worked configuration, an LGM to present-day deglaciation, is in examples/deglac_lgm.nml.

title: Installation and running
text:
Running with runme
runme stages a clean run directory (linking in data and input, copying the namelist, recording the parameters), then runs or submits it. The executable aliases match the drivers: main → vilma.x, mkref → vilma_mkref.x, remap → vilma_remap.x, visc3d → bench_visc3d.x.
# single local run, 8 OpenMP threads, overriding a few parameters
runme -o runs/deglac -e main --omp 8 -r \
      -p vilma.lmax=128 vilma.earth_response=ve ctl.file_out=out.nc
How a run is launched is set by two flags:

-r runs the executable;
-s prepares a SLURM submit script (and submits it, with -r);
-s -r prepares and submits on HPC; -s alone stages the script to inspect; omitting both stages the run directory only.

A comma list, range, or distribution in -p turns a parameter into an ensemble dimension (-p vilma.lmax=64,128), with -a naming the member directories from their parameter values.
SLURM settings live in .runme/config.toml, which is not tracked. Copy .runme/config.default.toml or run runme config init, then set the cluster (hpc, a key of runme queues --all) and the account; runme info shows what runme reads. On albedo:
hpc     = "awi_albedo"
account = "<project>"        # e.g. the p_forclima project account
omp     = 32
runme -o runs/deglac_lgm -e main -n examples/deglac_lgm.nml --omp 32 \
      -q 12h -w 06:00:00 -s -r -p vilma.lmax=128
On levante (hpc = "dkrz_levante", account = "<project>"):
runme -o runs/deglac_lgm -e main -n examples/deglac_lgm.nml --omp 64 \
      -q compute -w 06:00:00 -s -r -p vilma.lmax=128

title: Installation and running
text:
Embedding in a host model
The CLIMBER-X coupling path uses the same code behind a single use vilma. The contract is narrow: the host passes ice thickness in and receives relative sea level and bedrock out, on its own grid. The model owns its Gauss grid and the host↔︎Gauss remap (built from the parameter record), and keeps all spherical-harmonic work inside (see Implementation):
use vilma
type(solid_earth) :: se
call vilma_par_load(se%par, "vilma.nml", defaults_file=DEFAULTS_FILE)  ! configuration lives in se%par
call solid_earth_init(se, z_bed_eq, h_ice_eq, grid=host_grid, time=t0)  ! Gauss grid + remap; clock at t0 [yr]
call solid_earth_spinup(se, h_ice_lgm)                ! optional LGM-memory spin-up (holds the clock)
do
   call solid_earth_update(se, h_ice, dt_yr)          ! advance dt_yr [years]
   ! ... read se%rsl, se%z_bed, se%dz_bed, se%dz_ss, se%C on the host grid ...
   ! ... rsl = se%dz_ss - se%dz_bed: the sea-surface change N + dphi and the bed change u ...
end do
call solid_earth_finalize(se)                         ! frees the grid too
use vilma is the only module a host needs: it exports the parameter record, solid_earth and its life cycle, the checks and the restart routines, and nothing internal. h_ice is the whole ice column; the model applies its own flotation rule to it. The model keeps its own clock: solid_earth_init sets it (time, default 0), each update advances it, and solid_earth_set_time relabels it without changing the state. A host never writes se%time. A negative dt_yr stops the run; dt_yr = 0 re-solves the surface fields under the ice passed in.
grid (a coords lon-lat grid) is optional: omit it when the fields are already on the model’s Gauss grid in the SHTns layout (rows north first). A grid that is the Gauss grid passes the fields through exactly, in its own row order (latitude ascending, as coords builds it, or descending). Any other global grid is remapped; a regional grid is refused. The host-grid fields are always in the order the host supplied; se%gg is the internal Gauss-grid state. The full prognostic state is persisted on restart (vilma_restart_write, vilma_restart_read), so a coupled run resumes bit for bit; the host-grid outputs are re-derived on read.
vilma_par_load overlays the user file on defaults_file; without it the user file must hold every &vilma parameter. A host that fills se%par in memory instead starts from the in-code defaults, which leave lmax unset. The rest of the interface:







Procedure
Use




solid_earth_check_solver(par)
validate solver (and that a "v1" build has VILMA1) before any work


solid_earth_set_time(se, time)
relabel the clock [yr] without changing the state


solid_earth_sync_host(se)
refresh the host-grid outputs from the Gauss-grid state


solid_earth_enable_visc_3d(se, sht)
switch to the 3-D memory advance, keeping the memory (e.g. after a 1-D spin-up); init calls it when l_visc_3d is on


solid_earth_host_check(w, I_g, C, F, msg, tol)
admissibility of host-resolved terms (tol default 1e-9)


vilma_restart_write(se, time, filename, folder, init)
write the full state; defaults ./vilma_restart.nc, init = .false. appends a snapshot


vilma_restart_read(se, filename, time, other_visc)
restore the state at time (default the last snapshot) into an initialized se


vilma_restart_time(filename)
time [yr] of the last snapshot


vilma_restart_compatible(se, filename, msg, other_visc)
the checks vilma_restart_read applies, without reading


vilma_write_step, vilma_write_horizontal
diagnostic output, as the standalone driver writes it


vilma_io_set_table(filename)
path of the variable table (default input/vilma-variables.md)


vilma_version
the model version string



Two files are read relative to the working directory: the variable table input/vilma-variables.md, which every output and restart write uses (set another path with vilma_io_set_table), and the remap-weight cache maps/, keyed by the grid dimensions and a hash of the axis values.

Host-resolved terms (optional)
A host that resolves the ice margin on its own grid, inside regions of weight \(w\), can pass on that grid, per unit cell area, the grounded-ice column \(I_g = w H f_g\), the ocean fraction \(C = w (1 - f_g)\) and the flooded-area fill \(F = w \zeta^{(0)} (C - C_\text{ref})\):
call solid_earth_init(se, z_bed_eq, h_ice_eq, grid, w=w, I_g=I_g, C=C)    ! reference terms
call solid_earth_spinup(se, h_ice_lgm, w, I_g, C, F)                      ! held over every pass
call solid_earth_update(se, h_ice, dt_yr, w, I_g, C, F)                   ! ramped like the ice
ok = solid_earth_host_check(w, I_g, C, F, msg)                            ! admissibility
Inside \(w\) the sea-level solve uses these terms. On \(1 - w\) it applies its own flotation and coastline rule, and h_ice, h_ice_eq are the ice of that part (cells with \(w = 1\) ignore them). The terms are all or none and fixed for the run. They cannot be combined with solver = "v1" or sle_fixed_ocean, and \(F\) enters only through the sub-grid term (sle_subgrid). Without them, or with \(w \equiv 0\), a run is bit-identical to one without. The terms are part of the restart. Details are in the sea-level equation page and in doc/design.md §15.

title: Benchmarks
text:
VILMA2 is validated against the published GIA community benchmarks: the Charles University / Spada et al. (2011) intercomparison (Spada et al. 2011), the sea-level-equation intercomparison of Martinec et al. (2018) (Martinec et al. 2018) and, for lateral viscosity, the low-viscosity-zone case of Weerdesteijn et al. (2023) (Weerdesteijn et al. 2023). Validation proceeds along a ladder. Each rung is an independent benchmark that exercises one more piece of physics, so a failure localizes to the rung just added.
Every benchmark is an executable test with a pass/fail exit. The pages below quote two numbers for each: the tolerance the test asserts, and the difference measured with the reference build (model 1790f86, ifx 2024.1, -Ofast -march=znver2, on the AWI cluster albedo). The tolerance is the claim the test suite protects. The measured difference shows how much margin there is.
The reference datasets are vendored in the repository under data/benchmarks/ with provenance and licensing in data/benchmarks/PROVENANCE.md. None of it is VILMA2 output.

title: Benchmarks
section: What is validated and what is open
text:
What is validated and what is open
Validated. The radial solver, the Maxwell time stepping, the spatial synthesis, the horizontal displacement, the sea-level equation with a fixed and a migrating coastline, the Liouville polar-motion solve and the laterally varying viscosity each pass a published benchmark at the tolerances above. The two migrating-coastline cases and the deep-basin fixed-ocean case agree with the reference to below 1 m in every field.
Open.

Case C2 of the sea-level benchmark. The model differs from the reference by a uniform 5.9 m in sea surface (4.9 % of the signal) and by a degree-1 pattern of about 7 m in uplift. The test passes only because its uplift and horizontal tolerances are 30 % and 35 %. The cause is not attributed (see Sea-level equation).
Love numbers \(k\) and \(\ell\) at high degree. They leave 1 % of the normal-mode table above degrees 96 and 144 at the default radial mesh, while \(h\) stays within 0.1 %. The error is second order in the element size and falls below 1 % to degree 256 with a mesh four times finer (see Love numbers). The asserted range of the test (degree 48) has not been extended.
The disc response at 100 kyr and the uplift rate are not compared (see Disc-load response).
Three-dimensional viscosity. The only comparison with other codes is the axisymmetric low-viscosity-zone case on a 200 yr time scale, and a deglaciation comparison with VILMA1. No multi-code benchmark of a realistic 3-D structure at glacial time scales has been run.
Toroidal flow. No community benchmark exercises it. It is checked by internal consistency, symmetry and scaling tests (see Toroidal flow) and by the VILMA1 comparison of the last deglaciation, and is on by default. Its effect there is up to 92 m of relative sea level locally, 2–3 m rms globally.
Rotation coupled to the sea-level equation has no published benchmark and is checked for consistency only.

title: Benchmarks
text:
How to read the rungs

Rungs 1–2 isolate the linear algebra and the radial physics: the transform, then the per-degree elastic and fluid Love numbers. The fluid limit of a homogeneous sphere is an analytic anchor (\(h_j\to-(2j+1)/3\), \(k_j\to-1\)).
Rung 3 integrates the per-degree response over a spatial load (the disc) and adds the time relaxation.
Rung 4 adds the horizontal displacement (case A) and then the full self-consistent sea-level equation: ocean function, mass conservation, coastline migration, flotation, and the sub-grid sloping coast.
Rung 5 adds the rotational feedback. It is on by default for real-Earth runs and off in the non-rotating benchmarks.
Rung 6 adds laterally varying viscosity.







NoteAnalytic and inter-code benchmarks



Rungs 2, 3 and 5 compare with normal-mode solutions, which are accurate to their tabulated digits at low degree. Rungs 4b and 6 are comparisons between numerical codes. The reference is one code’s output, and the published scatter between codes (a few percent) bounds what agreement can show.

title: Benchmarks
text:
Running the benchmarks
make check                  # the fast suite: rungs 1–3, 4a, 5 and the unit tests
make openmp=1 check-slow    # rungs 4b and 6, test_rotinv at lmax 128, and three order tests
Both targets run every test, print a summary that names the failing tests, and return a non-zero exit status if any failed. check-slow takes about ten minutes on 32 threads. It raises the stack limit itself, since the 3-D path at \(\ell_\max \ge 128\) needs more than the default 8 MB per thread.

Dumping the comparison data
The benchmark tests can write the numbers behind their comparison. Set the environment variable VILMA_BENCH_DUMP to an existing directory, and each test writes plain-text column tables there (model and reference values on the reference abscissa, with a header line naming the columns):
mkdir -p dump
VILMA_BENCH_DUMP=$PWD/dump bin/test_benchmark_love.x
VILMA_BENCH_DUMP=$PWD/dump bin/test_benchmark_sle.x E2
Without the variable the tests write nothing. The figures on the benchmark pages are made from these tables by the scripts in the repository’s validation/ directory.

This benchmark tests the per-degree radial solver in isolation: for a unit surface load at degree \(j\), do the elastic (instantaneous) and fluid (fully relaxed) loading Love numbers match the reference?

title: Benchmark: Love numbers
text:
Earth model
M3–L70–V01 — incompressible, self-gravitating, layered Maxwell:

a 70 km elastic lithosphere (\(\eta\to\infty\)),
three viscous mantle layers,
an inviscid fluid core (\(\mu=0\)).

The layer table (radius, density, shear modulus, viscosity) is the incompressible model of the Spada et al. (2011) benchmark. VILMA2’s vilma_earth_structure reproduces the benchmark’s interface gravities, total mass, and moment of inertia as an independent check before any Love number is computed.

title: Benchmark: Love numbers
text:
Definitions
For a degree-\(j\) surface load of coefficient \(\sigma\), with the load’s own surface potential \(\varphi^{L} = 4\pi G\,a\,\sigma/(2j+1)\), the loading Love numbers are extracted from the surface radial functions (Farrell 1972 normalization, (Farrell 1972)):
\[
h_j = \frac{g_0(a)\,U(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
\ell_j = \frac{g_0(a)\,V(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
k_j = -\frac{F(a)}{\varphi^{L}} - 1.
\]
The \(-1\) in \(k_j\) follows from Martinec’s \(\varphi_1 = F\) being the total perturbation potential, which carries the load’s direct potential with the opposite sign to \(\varphi^{L}\) (\(F\to-\varphi^{L}\) for a rigid sphere).

title: Benchmark: Love numbers
text:
Analytic anchors
Two limits are exact and are checked first (test_love, to an absolute \(10^{-3}\) for the fluid limit and \(10^{-4}\) for the rigid limit):

Fluid (\(\mu\to 0\), homogeneous): \(h_j\to-(2j+1)/3\), \(k_j\to-1\).
Rigid (\(\mu\to\infty\)): \(h_j,\ell_j,k_j\to 0\).

The fluid limit independently exercises self-gravity, incompressibility, the Poisson coupling, and the load forcing; the rigid limit checks the shear block and the \(F\) sign.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
text: VILMA2 computes how the solid Earth and sea level respond to a changing load of ice and ocean water. This page introduces the ideas behind the model, one at a time, for a reader who is new to glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) or to this code. Each section gives the physical idea, its central equation and a short note on where it lives in VILMA2. The detailed derivations, parameters and validation are on the linked pages. The page assumes some familiarity with linear algebra and partial differential equations, and nothing about the code.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
text:
Refreshers and name origins
Two mathematical ideas recur throughout the model. The first is diagonalization. A linear operator \(L\) is diagonal in a basis of its eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\), since \(L\phi_k = \lambda_k\phi_k\). A field expanded in that basis, \(f = \sum_k c_k\phi_k\), then transforms coefficient by coefficient, \(Lf = \sum_k \lambda_k c_k\phi_k\). A coupled problem thus splits into many small, independent ones. This is the reason spherical harmonics are used horizontally (see below).
The second is fixed-point (Picard) iteration. An equation of the form \(x = F(x)\) is solved by repeating \(x_{k+1} = F(x_k)\) from a first guess. The sequence converges when \(F\) is a contraction, and it needs only evaluations of \(F\), not its Jacobian. The sea-level equation and its coupling to rotation and to the viscoelastic memory are all solved this way.
Several terms carry the names of their originators. The dimensionless response coefficients of a self-gravitating sphere are named after A. E. H. Love, who introduced them in Some Problems of Geodynamics (1911). The horizontal displacement number was added by T. Shida in 1912. The spring-and-damper rheology of the mantle is named after J. C. Maxwell, who proposed it in 1867. The sea-level equation in its modern form goes back to Farrell and Clark (1976).

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
section: The mantle as a Maxwell body
text:
The mantle as a Maxwell body
On the timescales of glacial cycles the mantle behaves as both a solid and a fluid. It responds elastically to a sudden change in load and flows viscously under a load that persists. A Maxwell body, an elastic spring and a viscous damper in series, captures both regimes with one constitutive law. For the deviatoric stress \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) and strain \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) it reads
\[
\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} + \frac{\mu}{\eta}\,\boldsymbol{\tau}
\;=\; 2\mu\,\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}},
\]
where \(\mu\) is the shear modulus and \(\eta\) the viscosity. Under a suddenly imposed strain the stress jumps to its elastic value and then decays on the Maxwell time
\[
\tau_M \;=\; \frac{\eta}{\mu}.
\]
For the upper mantle of the benchmark earth model M3–L70–V01 (\(\eta = 10^{21}\) Pa s, \(\mu \approx 7\times10^{10}\) Pa), \(\tau_M\) is about 450 yr. A load that changes faster than this sees a largely elastic mantle, while a load held for many Maxwell times sees a fluid one. Glacial cycles span both regimes, so both must be represented in the same simulation.
The real mantle is not a single Maxwell body. It is a stack of layers, each with its own density, shear modulus and viscosity, beneath an elastic lithosphere and above a fluid core. The relaxation of the surface is therefore not set by one Maxwell time. It is set by the whole structure, including the buoyancy of the displaced material, and it typically spans hundreds to many thousands of years. Viscosity may also vary laterally, for example between cratons and tectonically active regions. This lateral structure is the main reason a time-domain method was chosen for VILMA2.






TipIn VILMA2



The layered structure is built in vilma_earth_structure and selected by earth: "M3-L70-V01" (default), "PREM" (density and shear modulus from incompressible PREM on a given layer geometry) or "custom" (the layer arrays r_bot, r_top, rho, mu, eta, rheology). An elastic layer (rheology = 0) is exactly elastic, and a fluid layer (rheology = 2) carries no shear stress. Lateral viscosity is off by default (l_visc_3d = .false.). When it is on, a \(\log_{10}\eta\) field is read from visc_3d_file, by default the Bagge et al. (2021) field of the FesmData store, and clamped to visc_log10_min–visc_log10_max (19.5 to 30). The model does not ship a viscosity file. See Rheology, and the 3-D viscosity input chain for the order in which the field is built.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
text:
Spherical harmonics diagonalize the Laplacian
Spherical harmonics are the natural basis for fields on a sphere. Any square-integrable field on the surface can be expanded as
\[
f(\theta,\phi) \;=\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} f_{\ell m}\,Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi),
\]
where the degree \(\ell\) sets the angular scale of a pattern and the order \(m\) distributes its nodal lines between latitude and longitude. Zonal harmonics (\(m = 0\)) vary only with latitude, while sectoral harmonics (\(|m| = \ell\)) vary only with longitude.
The use of this basis follows from one property. The spherical harmonics are the eigenfunctions of the angular part of the Laplacian,
\[
\nabla_1^2\,Y_{\ell m} \;=\; -\,\ell(\ell+1)\,Y_{\ell m}.
\]
The Laplacian is thus diagonal in this basis, as described above. For a radially symmetric Earth the field equations of a loaded, self-gravitating sphere (momentum balance, Poisson’s equation and incompressibility) decouple degree by degree. Each degree \(\ell\) reduces to an independent radial problem, and the order \(m\) enters only through the load coefficients. The operator of a degree is therefore the same for all its orders.
In practice the expansion is truncated at a maximum degree \(\ell_\max\). The shortest resolved half-wavelength is about \(\pi a/\ell_\max\), where \(a\) is the radius of the Earth. This gives roughly 310 km at \(\ell_\max = 64\) and 120 km at \(\ell_\max = 170\), the resolution of VILMA1 in CLIMBER-X. The number of coefficients grows as \((\ell_\max+1)^2\), so the cost rises steeply with resolution.






TipIn VILMA2



vilma_sht wraps the SHTns library (Schaeffer 2013) and FFTW for the transforms between the Gauss–Legendre grid and spectral space. The harmonics are real and fully normalized, without the Condon–Shortley phase. The truncation is set by lmax (64 in input/vilma_defaults.nml, while a host must set it itself), and the grid by nlat and nphi (0 gives the de-aliased defaults \(2\ell_\max+2\) and \(4\ell_\max\)). SHTns is initialized without its per-grid algorithm tuning. This is fixed in vilma_sht at compile time and is not a run-time option. See Spectral reduction and Radial finite elements.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
section: Load Love numbers, one response per degree
text:
Load Love numbers, one response per degree
For a radially symmetric Earth the response to a surface load depends only on the degree of the load, not on its order. A load coefficient \(\sigma_{\ell m}\) therefore produces a vertical displacement, a horizontal displacement and a perturbation of the gravitational potential that are fixed multiples of it. These multiples are the load Love numbers \(h_\ell\), \(l_\ell\) and \(k_\ell\), respectively. Following Farrell (1972) they are defined relative to the potential of the load itself, \(\varphi^L = 4\pi G a\,\sigma/(2\ell+1)\):
\[
h_\ell = \frac{g_0\,U(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
l_\ell = \frac{g_0\,V(a)}{\varphi^{L}}, \qquad
k_\ell = -\frac{F(a)}{\varphi^{L}} - 1,
\]
where \(U(a)\) and \(V(a)\) are the radial and horizontal displacement at the surface, \(F(a)\) is the incremental potential there and \(g_0\) is surface gravity. The term \(-1\) in \(k_\ell\) removes the direct potential of the load, so that \(k_\ell\) describes only the deformation.
For a viscoelastic Earth the Love numbers become functions of time. A load applied at \(t = 0\) produces an instantaneous elastic response, which then relaxes toward the fluid limit as the mantle flows. For a homogeneous fluid sphere this limit is known exactly, \(h_\ell \to -(2\ell+1)/3\) and \(k_\ell \to -1\), which makes it a useful test of any GIA code.
Classical normal-mode codes write this time dependence as an elastic term plus a finite sum of exponentially decaying modes (Peltier 1974). The modes are found once per degree, and the response to an arbitrary load history then follows by convolution. This is efficient for a radially symmetric Earth. However, it cannot represent lateral viscosity, which couples the degrees and removes the per-degree response on which the method rests.
VILMA2 therefore does not compute modes. It solves the radial problem of each degree directly in time, following Martinec (2000), so the Love numbers are not inputs to the model. They are diagnostics that emerge from it: the first step gives the elastic response, and a load held long enough gives the fluid limit. The same per-degree solve then serves the 1-D and the 3-D case.






TipIn VILMA2



The radial problem of each degree is discretized with finite elements in vilma_radial_fe, which also holds the Love-number extraction (loading_love, tidal_love). The operator of each degree is factored once by the banded solver in vilma_band and reused at every step. vilma_response wraps the per-degree solves as a response operator, selected by earth_response: "ve" (viscoelastic, default), "elastic" or "null". The elastic \(h_\ell\) of M3–L70–V01 matches the reference table to within 0.08 % up to degree 256 (see Love numbers).

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
section: The sea-level equation and its fingerprint
text:
The sea-level equation and its fingerprint
Sea-level change caused by a melting ice sheet is not uniform. The meltwater raises the global mean, but the loss of ice mass also lowers the geoid near the ice sheet and lets the bed rebound there. Relative sea level therefore falls near a shrinking ice sheet and rises by more than the mean far from it. This spatial pattern is the sea-level fingerprint of the ice sheet.
The sea-level equation computes this pattern self-consistently. With the ocean function \(C\) (1 over ocean, 0 over land and grounded ice), the relative sea-level change \(S\) is
\[
S \;=\; C\cdot\bigl(N - u + \Delta\phi\bigr),
\]
where \(N\) is the geoid change, \(u\) the vertical displacement of the bed and \(\Delta\phi\) a spatially uniform term. The Earth responds to the total surface load,
\[
L \;=\; \rho_{\text{ice}}\,\Delta I \;+\; \rho_{\text{water}}\,C\cdot S,
\]
with \(\Delta I\) the change in grounded ice thickness. The uniform term \(\Delta\phi\) is chosen such that the ocean gains exactly the mass the ice loses. Since \(S\) appears in its own load, the equation is implicit. It is solved by fixed-point iteration: a guess of \(S\) gives the load, the load gives \(N\) and \(u\), and these give an updated \(S\).
Two refinements matter for realistic geometries. First, the coastline migrates. As sea level changes, land floods or emerges and grounded ice may float, so the ocean function itself must be updated. Second, a newly flooded cell does not fill instantly to the full sea-level change, and loading it as if it did puts a spurious step at the shoreline. The first refinement follows Kendall et al. (2005), and the second follows Martinec et al. (2018).






TipIn VILMA2



vilma_sle solves the equation in the pseudo-spectral form of Kendall et al. (2005): the response is applied in spectral space, and the product with the ocean function is formed on the grid. An inner loop iterates \(S\) at a fixed coastline (sle_n_inner = 20, sle_tol = \(10^{-7}\)), and an outer loop migrates the coastline (sle_n_outer = 3). The coastline migrates by default (sle_fixed_ocean = .false.), and newly flooded cells are loaded by their actual water column (sle_subgrid = .true.). Ocean mass is conserved by construction. The densities default to rho_ice = 917 and rho_water = 1000 kg m\(^{-3}\). Against the Martinec et al. (2018) cases D3, E2 and F1 the model agrees to within about 8 % of peak in every field. Case C2 shows an offset that is not yet attributed. See Sea-level equation and its benchmark.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
section: Off-axis mass drives the rotation pole
text:
Off-axis mass drives the rotation pole
A redistribution of surface mass changes the inertia tensor of the Earth and thereby moves its rotation axis. Mass placed away from the poles and the equator perturbs the off-diagonal products of inertia, and the pole drifts in response. This true polar wander changes the centrifugal potential, which acts as a further load on the Earth and on the ocean. This feedback has no global mean. Instead, it shifts sea level in a characteristic degree-2, order-1 pattern.
On GIA timescales the Chandler wobble can be neglected. The polar motion \(\mathbf{m}\) then follows the quasi-static linearized Liouville equation (Martinec and Hagedoorn 2014),
\[
\Bigl[\,1 - \tfrac{k^{T}(t)}{k_{s}}\,\Bigr] * \mathbf{m}(t) \;=\; \frac{I(t)}{C-A},
\]
where \(*\) is a convolution in time, \(I\) is the inertia perturbation including the deformation of the Earth, \(k^T\) is the degree-2 tidal Love number, \(k_s\) the secular (fluid-limit) Love number and \(C-A\) the difference between the polar and equatorial moments of inertia. The centrifugal potential of the displaced pole,
\[
\Lambda \;=\; -\Omega^{2}a^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta\,(m_1\cos\phi + m_2\sin\phi),
\]
is a degree-2, order-1 field. It enters the sea-level equation as one more contribution to the sea surface, so no separate solver is needed.






TipIn VILMA2



vilma_rotation carries two degree-2 viscoelastic channels (one forced by the load, one by the centrifugal potential) on the same radial operator as the load response. The rotation and the sea level are iterated to a common fixed point inside vilma_sle. Rotation is on by default (l_rotation = .true.) and is switched off for the non-rotating community benchmarks. rotation_k_s = 0 (default) uses the model’s own fluid limit for \(k_s\), and rotation_c_minus_a sets \(C-A\) (default \(2.63\times10^{35}\) kg m\(^2\)). The polar motion matches Spada test 3/2 to within 0.9 %. See Rotation and its benchmark.

title: Tutorial: the deforming Earth
text:
Explicit memory and time stepping
VILMA2 advances the Maxwell rheology explicitly in time. The total stress at a step is the elastic stress of the current strain plus a memory stress \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^V\) that carries the relaxation history. In the default scheme it is updated as
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} \;=\; (1-M)\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1}
\;-\; 2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\,i},
\qquad
M \;=\; \frac{\mu\,\Delta t}{\eta},
\]
where \(i\) is the step index and \(M\) is the Maxwell number of the step (Martinec 2000). The memory stress enters only the right-hand side of the field equations. The left-hand operator is therefore independent of time, of the time step and of viscosity. It is factored once per degree, and each step costs a back-substitution.
This choice has two consequences. First, lateral viscosity changes only the scalar \(M\), which multiplies known fields pointwise. The memory advance is then done on the grid and transformed back to spectral space, while the solve stays decoupled by degree. Second, the scheme is only conditionally stable. The step must satisfy \(\Delta t < 2\eta_{\min}/\mu\), so the lowest viscosity present sets the step. At the default floor of \(10^{19.5}\) Pa s and \(\mu \approx 7\times10^{10}\) Pa the limit \(M \le 1\) is about 15 yr. The coupling interval of a host model is thus split into shorter sub-steps, with the ice load interpolated linearly across the interval.
A second, implicit scheme is available. The trapezoidal (Crank–Nicolson) update is second-order accurate and A-stable, so its step is limited by accuracy rather than stability. Its step size is chosen adaptively, by comparing one full step with two half steps. Since the end-of-step strain depends on the end-of-step memory, each step is iterated together with the sea-level equation.






TipIn VILMA2



The memory scheme is selected by scheme: "fe" (explicit, default), with equal sub-steps at \(M \le\) cfl (default 1), or "trap" (trapezoidal, adaptive), with the tolerances rtol = \(10^{-4}\) and atol = \(10^{-3}\). The sub-step controller is vilma_timestep, the per-degree Maxwell kernel is in vilma_viscoelastic, and the field driver is in vilma_response. A host advances the model with solid_earth_update(se, h_ice, dt_yr) from vilma_coupling, which passes the coupling interval in years. With lateral viscosity the toroidal field is carried by default (l_toroidal = .true.). A deglaciation at \(\ell_\max = 170\) with 3-D viscosity then takes about 2.7 min of wall time per kyr on 64 threads (see Toroidal flow). A restarted run reproduces an uninterrupted one bit for bit. See Rheology and Time stepping.

title: The sea-level equation
text: Surface loading and sea level are coupled: ice and ocean water deform and re-gravitate the solid Earth, which moves the geoid and the solid surface, which redistributes the ocean water, which changes the load. VILMA2 solves this self-consistently with the migrating-coastline sea-level equation (SLE) in the pseudo-spectral form of Kendall et al. (2005), driven by the viscoelastic response operator.

title: The sea-level equation
text:
The response operator
The SLE is built on a thin abstraction. A response operator maps a spectral surface-mass load \(\sigma_{\ell m}\) to the surface uplift \(u_{\ell m}\) and geoid height \(N_{\ell m}\):
\[
\texttt{apply}:\ \sigma_{\ell m}\ \longmapsto\ (u_{\ell m},\ N_{\ell m}).
\]
The geoid is obtained from the incremental potential by Bruns’ formula, \(N(a) = -F(a)/g\), where \(F\) is the radial coefficient of \(\varphi_1\). This uses only \(U\) and \(F\) — not the horizontal Love number \(\ell\) — so the SLE is never blocked by horizontal-displacement conventions. Three implementations share the interface:








Implementation
Response
Use




elastic_response
per-degree elastic gains \(g_u(\ell), g_N(\ell)\)
instantaneous Earth


null_response
\(u\equiv N\equiv 0\)
rigid, non-self-gravitating \(\to\) eustatic baseline


ve_response
viscoelastic field driver (memory history per \((\ell,m)\))
the GIA case

title: The sea-level equation
text:
The sea-level equation
Let \(C(\theta,\phi)\) be the ocean function (1 over ocean, 0 over land/grounded ice), \(\Delta I\) the ice-thickness change, and \(S\) the relative sea-level change. The SLE is a Fredholm equation of the second kind,
\[
S \;=\; C\cdot\bigl(N - u + \Delta\phi\bigr),
\]
where \((N,u)\) is the Earth’s response to the total load \(L = \rho_{\text{ice}}\,\Delta I + \rho_{\text{water}}\,C\!\cdot\!S\), and the spatial constant \(\Delta\phi\) enforces conservation of ocean mass,
\[
\rho_{\text{water}}\!\int C\!\cdot\!S\,\mathrm{d}A
\;=\; -\,\rho_{\text{ice}}\!\int_{\text{grounded}} \Delta I\,\mathrm{d}A .
\]
Fixing \(\Delta\phi\) each iteration from this balance makes mass exactly conserved by construction (to machine precision), rather than as a converged residual.

title: The sea-level equation
text:
Pseudo-spectral fixed-point iteration
The equation is solved by nested fixed-point iteration (Kendall et al. 2005):

Inner loop — iterate \(S\) at a fixed coastline. The load \(\to\) response convolution is done in spectral space (it is diagonal per degree), while the ocean-function product \(C\!\cdot\!S\) is formed pointwise on the Gauss–Legendre grid. Mixing the two representations this way is what kills the Gibbs ringing that a purely spectral coastline product would produce.
Outer loop — migrate the coastline by recomputing the ocean function from the updated topography \(\text{topo}_0 - S\), then repeat.

The inner loop stops when the change of \(C\!\cdot\!S\) falls below sle_tol (default \(10^{-7}\)) relative to its maximum, or after sle_n_inner iterations (default 20). The outer loop stops when the updated sea level implies the same ocean function, or after sle_n_outer passes (default 3). Each solve starts from the relative sea level of the previous one, which shortens the inner loop. With a viscoelastic response and scheme = "trap", a third loop around both re-converges the load against the end-of-step memory (sle_max_mem_iter, see Time stepping). The densities are rho_ice (default 917 kg m\(^{-3}\)) and rho_water (default 1000 kg m\(^{-3}\)). A host with its own densities sets both.

title: The sea-level equation
section: Ocean function, flotation, and the coast
text:
Ocean function, flotation, and the coast
The ocean function distinguishes three regimes, each handled explicitly so that no mass is double-counted:

Grounded vs. floating ice. A cell is ocean only where it is below sea level and the ice does not ground: \(\rho_{\text{ice}}\,I < -\rho_{\text{water}}\,\text{topo}\). Only grounded ice loads the bed and changes the ocean-water budget; floating ice is already carried by the ocean term. The grounded-ice increment is therefore the difference of the two grounded columns, each masked by its own ocean function, \(\Delta I_g = I\,(1-C) - I_0\,(1-C_0)\). Masking the raw increment by the current \(C\) alone, \((I-I_0)(1-C)\), would drop the whole column of marine-grounded reference ice from the melt source when its cell floods.
Two ocean-geometry modes. The migrating coastline (SLE2) updates \(C\) every outer iteration. It is the default (sle_fixed_ocean = .false.). A fixed ocean (Martinec SLE1, sle_fixed_ocean = .true.) holds \(C\) at the ocean function of the reference state for the whole run.
Sub-grid (sloping-coast) loading. The binary load \(\rho_{\text{water}}\,C\!\cdot\!S\) puts the full sea-level change wherever \(C=1\), giving a sharp shoreline. The sub-grid mode (sle_subgrid, on by default) instead loads the actual water-column change \(s = C\!\cdot\!S - \zeta^{(0)}(C - C_0)\), which tapers smoothly to zero as a newly flooded cell fills from its own bed (Martinec 2018, §2.2, eqs. 15–19). The fill term \(\int\zeta^{(0)}(C - C_0)\,\mathrm{d}A\) then also enters the mass balance that fixes \(\Delta\phi\). This is a local correction — one extra field term and one integral — yet it collapses the cap-edge grounding-line residuals in the migrating benchmark cases to the \(\sim 1\%\) level.

title: The sea-level equation
text:
Host-resolved terms
A host model that resolves the ice margin on its own, finer grid can pass the result instead of leaving flotation to the Gauss grid. This is optional. For the part \(w\) of each Gauss cell that its regions cover, the host passes the grounded-ice column \(I_g = w H f_g\), the ocean fraction \(C = w(1-f_g)\) and the flooded-area fill \(F = w\,\zeta^{(0)}(C - C_{\text{ref}})\), all per unit cell area (\(f_g\) is the grounded fraction). The sea-level solve uses these terms inside \(w\) and applies its own flotation and coastline rule on the remaining \(1-w\). The terms are given at initialization (the reference: \(w\), \(I_g\), \(C\)) and at every update, and they ramp over the coupling interval like the ice. They are given for the whole run or not at all. With no terms, or \(w \equiv 0\), the results are those of a run without them, bit for bit (test_host_bitident). The standalone driver does not use them.






NoteWhy the affine trick makes the VE driver tractable



The viscoelastic response at a fixed time is affine in the current load: \(u_{\ell m} = g_u(\ell)\,\sigma_{\ell m} + \text{drift}_{\ell m}\), where the drift comes from the frozen past-relaxation memory. So the SLE fixed point can call apply() as many times as it likes within a step without corrupting the Maxwell state. A begin_step freezes the drift (one memory-forcing solve per coefficient); the memory is then advanced once, with the converged load. This is what lets a viscoelastic Earth sit inside an iterative SLE solver cheaply.

title: The sea-level equation
text:
Reference frame and degree 1
The geocenter (degree-1) terms are physical and frame-dependent. The radial solve fixes the rigid-translation null space with a gauge (zero volume-integrated displacement, a centre-of-figure-like frame; see Radial finite elements). Since a rigid translation carries no strain, the frame can then be changed after the solve by adding a multiple of the null mode. deg1_frame selects the frame:

In "cm" the CM condition is imposed once, on the solved state, so displacement and geoid refer to the same frame and the relative sea level carries the degree-1 fingerprint of geocenter motion (Blewitt 2003). This reduces the disc residual against VILMA1 about fivefold. "cf" is the mixed convention of the Spada (2011) disc benchmark, displacement in a CE-like gauge (\(h_1\approx 0\)) and geoid in CM (\(N_1 = 0\)), under which rsl has no degree-1 part. Degrees \(\ge 2\) are identical in both frames. See the disc benchmark.






TipWhere this lives in the code



vilma_response defines the response-operator interface and its three implementations; vilma_sle is the fixed-point SLE solver (ocean function, flotation, migration, sub-grid load, mass-conserving \(\Delta\phi\)); vilma_field builds analytic ice caps and basin topographies for the benchmarks. Validation is in Sea-level equation.

title: Rotational feedback (polar motion)
text: A redistribution of surface mass (ice, ocean water) and the resulting solid-Earth deformation change the planet’s inertia tensor, which perturbs the rotation vector — true polar wander (TPW). The shifted rotation in turn alters the centrifugal potential, itself a degree-2 surface load that drives further deformation and sea-level change. VILMA2 implements this two-way rotational feedback in the time domain, consistent with the explicit memory-stress machinery.

title: Rotational feedback (polar motion)
text:
Formulation
The rotational theory follows the time-domain approach of Martinec and Hagedoorn (2014), which composes with a viscoelastic, 3D-viscosity solver. On the GIA timescale the Chandler wobble is neglected, leaving a quasi-static Liouville equation for the polar-motion vector \(\mathbf{m}\),
\[
\Bigl[\,1 - \tfrac{k^{T}(t)}{k_{s}}\,\Bigr] * \mathbf{m}(t) = \Psi_{L}(t),
\qquad
\Psi_{L}(t) = \frac{I(t)}{C-A},
\qquad
I(t) = \bigl[\delta(t) + k^{L}(t)\bigr] * I_{\rm rigid}(t),
\]
where \(*\) is time convolution, \(I_{\rm rigid}\) is the rigid-body inertia perturbation from the surface load, \(k^{L}\) and \(k^{T}\) are the loading and tidal degree-2 Love numbers, \(k_s\) is the secular (fluid-limit) number, and \(C-A\) is the moment difference.
The implementation carries two degree-2 viscoelastic channels on the same per-degree operator — a loading channel forced by the rigid inertia (from the load’s (2,1) spherical-harmonic coefficient, i.e. Gauss quadrature of the actual load, so no axisymmetry is assumed) and a tidal channel forced by the centrifugal potential. Each carries its own Maxwell memory. Both channels are radially symmetric and relax on the same radial viscosity as the load response: a viscosity file’s radial profile, taking the lateral geometric mean where the file varies laterally, and the layer table only when no file is read. The polar motion \(\mathbf{m}\) is solved algebraically each step and is affine in the load, so it sits inside the SLE ↔︎ rotation fixed point safely; the channel memories are committed once with the converged \(\mathbf{m}\).

title: Rotational feedback (polar motion)
text:
Coupling through the sea-level equation
The centrifugal potential of the perturbed rotation,
\[
\Lambda = -\Omega^{2} a^{2}\,\sin\theta\cos\theta\,(m_1\cos\phi + m_2\sin\phi),
\]
is a degree-2, order-1 field. It is the first-order change of \(\tfrac12\Omega^2 a^2\sin^2\theta'\) about the displaced pole \(\hat z + m_1\hat x + m_2\hat y\): a point the pole moves toward comes closer to the spin axis, so sea level falls there. It enters the SLE as the rotational sea-surface contribution \(s_{\rm rot} = (1+k^{T})\Lambda/g - h^{T}\Lambda/g\) (geoid minus uplift). The rotation steps with the solid Earth: inside every SLE solve, each iteration’s load sets the polar motion at the end of that solver sub-step, and its \(s_{\rm rot}\) enters the same iteration’s sea surface, so the rotation ↔︎ SLE fixed point converges together with the sea level. The channels are committed where the load response’s memory advances. A sub-step longer than the channels’ explicit stability limit is sub-cycled with the load held. The rotational potential is thus treated as a load like any other — self-consistent, not a bolt-on correction.

title: Rotational feedback (polar motion)
text:
Design constraints honoured

Degree-2, tidal Love numbers. The rotational deformation uses tidal (not loading) Love numbers; the centrifugal forcing is purely degree 2.
The secular number \(k_s\). By default \(k_s\) is the model’s own fluid limit \(k^T_f\): the tidal response with every Maxwell layer fluidized, which reproduces Spada test 3/2. Deriving \(k_s\) from the assumed lithosphere thickness leads to the well-known “lithosphere-thickness paradox” in rotational stability. The observed-flattening value \(k_s = 3G(C-A)/(a^5\Omega^2)\) (Mitrovica et al. 2005), recommended for deep time, is computed as well. rotation_k_s (> 0) prescribes \(k_s\) and rotation_c_minus_a sets \(C-A\).
Couple through the SLE. The rotational potential enters the sea-level equation self-consistently (above).

title: Rotational feedback (polar motion)
text:
Validation
The Liouville polar-motion solve is checked against Spada et al. (2011) test 3/2 (Spada et al. 2011). The polar motion of a cap and a disc load matches Table 14 of that paper to better than 1 % at all six tabulated times (see the rotation benchmark). For M3–L70–V01 the model’s fluid limit is \(k_s = 0.967\), and the observed-flattening value is 0.944.
No published benchmark covers the sea-level equation with rotation. The rotation ↔︎ SLE fixed point is therefore checked for consistency by test_rotation_sle: ocean mass conservation, the elastic relation of the rotational field, the direction of the pole shift, sub-cycling and the save/restore round trip.






TipWhere this lives in the code



vilma_rotation holds the two degree-2 channels, the Liouville solve, and the s_rot SLE contribution; vilma_sle iterates the rotation ↔︎ SLE fixed point and vilma_timestep steps and rolls it back with the load response; vilma_io persists the polar motion and channel memory on restart. On by default (l_rotation = .true.); set l_rotation = .false. for non-rotating benchmarks.

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
text: After the spectral reduction, each spherical-harmonic degree \(j\) is an independent 1D radial boundary-value problem. VILMA2 discretizes it with finite elements in radius, assembling the symmetric saddle-point operator that is the Hessian of the energy functional.

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
text:
Mesh and bases
The mesh spans the whole sphere \(\langle 0, a\rangle\) — the inviscid core is meshed too — with piecewise-constant \(\rho_k,\mu_k\) per element. Each element’s size follows the target for its own depth (default 5 km above 70 km, 10 km to 670 km, 40 km below, after VEGA; namelist mesh_dr, mesh_depth, mesh_dr_scale). Layer interfaces are always nodes, and within a layer the elements share \(\int \mathrm{d}r/h\) equally, so a thick layer is meshed like a stack of thin ones. M3–L70–V01 uses 218 nodes (217 elements), the 11-layer PREM 220 nodes (219 elements).

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
section: A symmetric operator — and the bug that hid in it
text:
A symmetric operator — and the bug that hid in it
Laid out node-interleaved as \([U\ V\ F\mid\Pi]\), the per-degree system is
\[
\begin{bmatrix} A & B^{\mathsf T}\\ B & 0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d\\ \Pi\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} f\\ 0\end{bmatrix},
\]
with \(A\) the shear+gravity stiffness and \(B\) the incompressibility coupling. The whole operator is symmetric — it is the second variation (Hessian) of the energy functional \(E\), hence self-transpose by construction. In particular the self-gravity \(U\!\leftrightarrow\! F\) coupling is a transpose pair: the potential-gradient body force \(\int\rho_0(\mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}r)\,\delta U\,r^2\) and the Poisson source \(\int\rho_0 U(\mathrm{d}\,\delta F/\mathrm{d}r)\,r^2\) discretize to \(I^2_{\beta\alpha}\) and \(I^2_{\alpha\beta}\) respectively.






WarningTypo in Martinec (2000), eq. (81)



The discretized self-gravity block written out in Martinec (2000) eq. (81) appears to contain a typo: it gives the \(U\)–\(F\) coupling as \(I^2_{\alpha\beta}\) where the symmetric partner \(I^2_{\beta\alpha}\) is required. Because the full operator is the Hessian of the energy functional \(E\), it must be symmetric; the corresponding term in the continuous form (eq. 65) makes this clear on term-by-term inspection. Using eq. (81) as written breaks the operator symmetry and softens the elastic low-degree Love numbers markedly — \(h_e(2)\) was \(\sim 47\%\) below the benchmark in our own tests, while every analytic limit and the fluid limit still passed. Anyone implementing this block should take eq. (65) as the arbiter, use \(I^2_{\beta\alpha}\) for the \(U\)–\(F\) coupling, and assert \(\lVert A - A^{\mathsf T}\rVert = 0\) on the assembled matrix.
crumbs: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
text:
Boundary and regularity conditions

Surface — the exterior potential match (\(\varphi_1\propto r^{-(j+1)}\) outside) adds a \((j+1)F(a)\) term on the \(F\!-\!F\) diagonal at the surface node; the load enters as the right-hand side \(-a^2\sigma\,g_0(a)\) on \(U(a)\) and \(-a^2\sigma\) on \(F(a)\) (eq. 84).
Centre \(r=0\) — no explicit BC (meshed through, \(r^2\) weighting + \(R_1=0\)).
Core–mantle boundary — none imposed; free-slip emerges from \(\mu=0\) in the meshed core.
Density-jump interfaces — natural conditions of the weak form.
crumbs: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
text:
Degree 1: the geocenter, kept sparse
Degree 1 carries the rigid-translation null space, removed by \(E_{\text{uniq}}\) (eq. 83). That penalty is a rank-1 term whose coefficient is \(\sim 10^{16}\times\) the band entries — i.e. it is already a hard constraint \(w^{\mathsf T}d = 0\) (zero volume-integrated displacement, a centre-of-figure-like gauge) in all but name. Imposing it as a dense penalty would fill the band; instead it borders the band with one KKT row/column:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} A_{\text{band}} & w\\ w^{\mathsf T} & 0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d\\ \lambda\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} f\\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The solve runs at \(\text{ndof}+1\) internally but keeps the physical \(\text{ndof}\) interface, so the time stepper needs no degree-1 special case. The same KKT system also yields the null mode itself (zero physical right-hand side, border value 1). Because a rigid translation carries no strain, the reference frame is a post-solve choice: adding a multiple of the null mode that makes the exterior degree-1 potential vanish, \(F_1(a) = 0\), puts the state in the CM frame (Blewitt 2003) (deg1_frame = "cm", the default). The geocenter is thus the physical degree-1 signal, not a hard-coded \(\{h_1,l_1,k_1\}\). See Sea-level equation.
crumbs: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator

title: Radial finite elements and the per-degree operator
text:
The toroidal operator
When the toroidal field is carried, \(W\) has its own per-degree operator rather than a fifth interleaved field: \(W\) couples to nothing else on the left-hand side, so the spheroidal band is untouched. It is the \(W\) part of the shear energy (eq. 80), assembled from the same \(I_1,I_3,I_6\) integrals. It is tridiagonal and symmetric, with fluid-core nodes pinned to \(W = 0\) and, at degree 1, one KKT border per solid shell removing the rigid rotation. See Toroidal flow.






TipWhere this lives in the code



vilma_radial_fe assembles build_dense_operator (the reference dense operator, with the dense \(E_{\text{uniq}}\) penalty for cross-checking) and the banded operator used in production; vilma_radial_integrals holds the Appendix-C element integrals. Love numbers are extracted by loading_love — see Love numbers. Validated by test_assembly, test_love.

title: Spectral reduction and the SH transform
text: Horizontally, every field is expanded in spherical harmonics; the angular dependence is handled analytically and each degree decouples. This page covers the spectral reduction of the field equations and the transform kernel that moves between grid and spectral space.
crumbs: Spectral reduction and the SH transform

title: Spectral reduction and the SH transform
text:
Vector spherical-harmonic expansion
The displacement, potential, and pressure are expanded as (Martinec 2000, eqs. 55–57)
\[
\mathbf{u} = \sum_{j\ge 1}\Bigl[\,U_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(-1)}_{jm}
+ V_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(1)}_{jm}
+ W_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(0)}_{jm}\,\Bigr],
\qquad
\varphi_1 = \sum_{j\ge 0} F_{jm}(r)\,Y_{jm},
\quad
\Pi = \sum_{j\ge 0}\Pi_{jm}(r)\,Y_{jm},
\]
where \(\mathbf{S}^{(-1)},\mathbf{S}^{(1)},\mathbf{S}^{(0)}\) are the spheroidal (radial, consoidal) and toroidal vector harmonics. Two simplifications follow from the physics:

No degree 0 in \(\mathbf{u}\) — incompressibility forbids the radial breathing mode.
The toroidal block decouples: \(W\) couples to nothing on the left-hand side (no pressure, self-gravity or \(U,V\) shear terms), so a surface load on a radially symmetric Earth never excites it. Laterally varying viscosity does, through the memory stress (Martinec 2000, after eq. 110); \(W\) is then solved by its own tridiagonal per-degree system alongside the spheroidal one (see Toroidal flow). The divergence reduces to \(\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u} = \sum (U' + 2U/r - J\,V/r)\,Y_{jm}\), \(J=j(j+1)\) (eq. 58).

Each degree \(j\) then reduces to an independent 1D radial problem in \(\{U_{jm},V_{jm},F_{jm},\Pi_{jm}\}\) — the central economy of the method. The order \(m\) enters only through the (real) load coefficients, so the operator is assembled and factored once per degree and reused across all \(m\).
crumbs: Spectral reduction and the SH transform

title: Spectral reduction and the SH transform
text:
Real, orthonormal harmonics
VILMA2 uses fully normalized real spherical harmonics with no Condon–Shortley phase, on a Gauss–Legendre latitude grid with a \(\phi\)-contiguous layout; spectral arrays store \(m \ge 0\). This convention (SHT_ORTHONORMAL, SHT_NO_CS_PHASE) is pinned across the whole code so that quadrature (\(\int\!\mathrm{d}\Omega\)), the orthonormality of \(Y_{10}\), and round-trip transforms all hold to machine precision.
crumbs: Spectral reduction and the SH transform

title: Spectral reduction and the SH transform
crumbs: Spectral reduction and the SH transform

title: Spectral reduction and the SH transform
text:
Resolution
The reference VILMA1-scale configuration is SH degree 170 with a \(1024\times 2048\) SLE grid. The benchmark cases here run at degree 32–128; the Love-number and disc benchmarks synthesize spatial profiles by summing the per-degree response against Legendre polynomials. All spherical-harmonic transforms stay inside this model — a host such as CLIMBER-X exchanges only grid-space ice thickness and bedrock/sea-level fields.

title: The banded direct solver and performance
text: The per-degree saddle-point system is small, banded, and reused unchanged across all orders \(m\), all loads, and every time step. VILMA2 therefore solves it with a dependency-free, re-entrant, pivoted banded LU — factor once, solve many times — which is both faster and structurally simpler than the iterative solver used in early versions.
crumbs: The banded direct solver and performance

title: The banded direct solver and performance
section: Why a banded direct solve fits
text:
Why a banded direct solve fits
Laid out node-interleaved as \([U\ V\ F\mid\Pi]\), the operator has a half-bandwidth of \(\sim 6\). Its entries span \(\sim 20\) orders of magnitude (\(\mu r^2/h\) versus the pressure couplings versus \(1/4\pi G\)), so it is first geometric-mean row/column equilibrated. Two facts then make a direct band solve ideal:

The operator depends on degree only through \(J = j(j+1)\), so it is assembled and factored once per degree and reused for all \(m\), all loads, and all time steps. A step costs only a band back-substitution.
It is indefinite (zero pressure block), so partial pivoting is required; the vilma_band LU pivots within the band.

Degree 1 carries the dense KKT border (the rigid-mode constraint), giving that one degree a near-full bandwidth — it factors as a dense LU through the same code path. The result is \(\sim 20\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) per solve, versus \(\sim 700\
\mu\mathrm{s}\) for the earlier iterative (GMRES+ILU) solver, with no preconditioner fill to evict from cache.
crumbs: The banded direct solver and performance

title: The banded direct solver and performance
text:
No external linear-algebra dependency
vilma_band is hand-rolled and dependency-free: it pulls in no LAPACK and no LIS. This is a deliberate design choice driven by linking into a larger, OpenMP-parallel host:






NoteWhy LIS (and LAPACK) were removed



An earlier version used the LIS iterative-solver library. Linking LIS into an OpenMP host (CLIMBER-X) would pull in lis-omp, nesting OpenMP regions, and concurrent LIS solves are not re-entrant (global solver state). The hand-rolled band LU has no global state, so it is re-entrant and the per-degree loop parallelizes cleanly with OpenMP. With LIS gone there is no serial-vs-OpenMP variant to reconcile. The project also avoids LAPACK for the same dependency-minimization reason — the band solver is small and fully tested (test_band against a dense reference).

title: Time stepping and the field driver
text: The viscoelastic evolution is an explicit march in time built directly on the elastic operator. This page covers how a step is taken, how the memory state is carried, and how the field-level driver feeds the sea-level equation without corrupting that state.
crumbs: Time stepping and the field driver

title: Time stepping and the field driver
text:
One step
The \(\omega=1\) Maxwell scheme (see Rheology) keeps the left-hand operator fixed and updates only the right-hand side. A step at degree \(j\) is:

Form the dissipative forcing \(-\int\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1}:\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) from the previous memory stress (a two-point radial Gauss quadrature of the spectral double-dot over the four spheroidal tensor components).
Add the surface-load right-hand side for the current load.
Back-substitute through the once-factored operator (no re-factorization).
Update the memory stress \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} = (1-M)\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1} - 2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i}\) from the new strain.

Elastic layers (\(M\to 0\)) freeze; fluid layers (\(\mu=0\)) carry no memory. The 1D validation test_relax shows a held load relaxing monotonically from the elastic Love number to the fluid limit \(-(2j+1)/3\), with \(t_{\text{relax}}\propto\eta\) and convergence under step refinement.
This explicit update is conditionally stable: the step is capped by the shortest Maxwell time, so a short dynamical \(\Delta t\) is sub-cycled within the coupling interval. The vilma_timestep controller sizes the sub-steps according to the memory scheme (see Rheology):

"fe" (default): the 1st-order update has no embedded error signal, so \(\Delta t\) is set a priori by the stability ceiling \(M = \mu\Delta t/\eta \le\) cfl (default 1; it must lie in (0, 2), the update’s stability range), taken over the fastest Maxwell rate present. The interval is split into equal sub-steps of at most that length. dt_max lowers the sub-step further. dt_min raises it, also above the stability ceiling, so it should stay at its default of 0 (none) for this scheme. A guard rolls a sub-step back and halves it if the memory norm becomes non-finite. It is a safety net and normally never fires.
"trap": each candidate step is taken once at \(\Delta t\) and once as two \(\Delta t/2\) halves. Their difference estimates the local error of the memory, which is compared with atol \(+\) rtol \(\times\) the memory norm (defaults \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-4}\)). A rejected step is rolled back and retried smaller. An accepted one keeps the fine result. The next step size follows from the error estimate with the factor safety (0.9). Its change is limited to between shrink_min (0.2) and grow_max (5), and its value to the range dt_min–dt_max. A step at dt_min is accepted even above tolerance. The first trial step is dt_init (default 0: the whole interval). The step size then carries over from one interval to the next.

The dt_* parameters are given in years. The coupling interval itself is not a parameter: the host, or the forcing time axis of the standalone driver, passes it with each update. The ice load is interpolated linearly between the interval endpoints. scheme is "fe" or "trap" (see Rheology).
crumbs: Time stepping and the field driver

title: Time stepping and the field driver
text:
The viscoelastic field driver
The SLE needs a field load whose every coefficient \((\ell,m)\) has its own independent load history — the ice and ocean evolve differently everywhere. The ve_response driver provides this while remaining safe to call from inside an iterative solver, using the affine structure of the response at fixed time:
\[
u_{\ell m} \;=\; g_u(\ell)\,\sigma_{\ell m} \;+\; \text{drift}_{\ell m},
\]
where \(g_u(\ell)\) is the instantaneous (elastic) gain and \(\text{drift}_{\ell m}\) comes from the frozen past-relaxation memory. The step is bracketed:

begin_step freezes the drift — one memory-forcing solve per coefficient, done once at the start of the step;
apply() is then a cheap affine evaluation the SLE fixed point may call repeatedly;
the memory advance then moves the Maxwell memory forward once, with the converged load.

The memory advance has two entry points. commit_step takes a given load and is used by the response-level tests. The sea-level solve instead uses prepare_endpoint, advance_endpoint and finalize_step, which let the load and the memory converge together. With scheme = "fe" both do one explicit update. With scheme = "trap" the update needs the end-of-step strain, so the step endpoint is iterated: the drift is re-solved against the trial \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i}\) until the surface drift stops changing (relative change below \(10^{-6}\)). In the sea-level solve the water load is re-converged in each of these passes, up to sle_max_mem_iter passes (default 20).
Each complex \((\ell,m)\) history is stored as two real histories (real/imaginary), since the operator and \(M=\mu\Delta t/\eta\) are real. The per-element Maxwell kernel is shared verbatim with the 1D stepper — test_ve_response confirms the field driver’s first step equals elastic_response exactly, and that a held degree-2 field reproduces the 1D ve_degree history to \(\sim 10^{-13}\).
crumbs: Time stepping and the field driver

title: Time stepping and the field driver
text:
Memory storage and restart
The per-\((\ell,m)\) memory and drift are stored in degree-grouped slot order (an \(\ell m \leftrightarrow k\) map), so the inner loop is contiguous and per-degree, allowing operator reuse without scattering the (large) memory arrays.
A restart file is written without rounding. It carries the following state:
