The memory stress is by far the largest part. The surface fields follow from the memory and the load, but they are restored as well: the ice is the start of the next load ramp, and the relative sea level seeds the next sea-level solve. The elastic and the null response carry no memory, so their restart holds the other rows only. The full variable table is input/vilma-variables.md.
The reference fields are static: the equilibrium bed and ice and, with host-resolved terms, the host reference. They are written once and compared with the initialized model on read. A mismatch stops the run. A file with host-resolved terms cannot be read into a run without them, nor the reverse.
A restart also records the Earth its memory belongs to: checksums of the radial mesh (mesh_checksum), of the radial viscosity (visc_radial_checksum) and of the 3-D field (visc_3d_checksum). A restart from another mesh is refused. A restart from another viscosity is refused too, unless restart_other_visc = .true. (&ctl): its memory then seeds the run (e.g. a 1-D spin-up for a 3-D run) rather than continuing it. Other parameters (the time scheme, the sea-level settings) are not checked.
A run resumes at the restart’s time. The driver starts the forcing window at that time, and a time_init that selects another start stops the run, so a restart cannot replay the forcing by mistake. restart_time_reset = .true. (&ctl) instead takes the restart’s state as the state at the start of the window, whatever time the file carries.
test_restart asserts that a restarted run reproduces an uninterrupted one bit for bit, with rotation on, for a radially symmetric Earth and for a 3-D field with toroidal channels. test_restart_3d asserts the same after the 1-D pre-spin-up, and test_restart_host covers host-resolved terms.
A lower-resolution restart can be read into a higher-resolution run. The memory of the shared low degrees is copied (a contiguous block in the degree-grouped order) and the higher degrees start at zero. The surface fields, the trapezoidal load and the host-resolved terms live on the file’s grid and are not transferred. The caller re-derives the surface fields with a zero-length update. A run can thus be spun up at coarse resolution and continued at fine resolution, but that continuation is not bit for bit. A higher-resolution file cannot be read into a lower-resolution run.
crumbs: Time stepping and the field driver

title: Time stepping and the field driver
text:
Coupling cadence
For host coupling (CLIMBER-X), the model sub-cycles its short dynamical step \(\Delta t\) within a longer coupling interval. The ice thickness ramps linearly from the previous update’s value to the new one across the interval. The SLE is solved each \(\Delta t\), and the bedrock \(z_{\text{bed}} = z_{\text{bed,eq}} - \text{rsl}\) is returned at the coupling cadence.
The reference state is the relaxed state. The memory is zero there, and relative sea level is measured against it. A host passes the reference at initialization. The standalone driver chooses it with i_eq (&ctl):







i_eq
Reference bed and ice




0
the start slice of the forcing


1 (default)
a present-day reference (z_bed_ref_file, h_ice_ref_file), so that rsl is close to zero at the present day


2
an equilibrium state read from z_bed_eq_file and h_ice_eq_file


3
the present-day reference bed plus an rsl field from rsl_restart_file




Spin-up
A run that starts away from the reference (a held LGM load, say) starts with zero memory, as if the load had just been applied. The optional spin-up (solid_earth_spinup) removes this. It holds the start-slice ice and relaxes the model toward isostatic equilibrium, with the reference kept as the datum. The transient then starts with viscous memory. The spin-up has two phases, both off by default:

Full-model phase (equil_time_max \(> 0\), in years). The held load is relaxed in passes of growing length: 200 yr first, then 1.6 times longer each pass, at most 60 passes. After each pass the mean bed velocity is the global mean of the absolute bed change over the pass, divided by the pass length. The phase ends when this falls below equil_rate_tol (default \(10^{-3}\) m/yr). equil_time_max caps the total relaxation time. If the cap is reached first, the run continues and prints a warning with the remaining rate.
1-D pre-phase (pre_spinup_1d = .true.). The same relaxation first runs on a laterally uniform field, the lateral mean of \(\log_{10}\eta\) of the 3-D field at each radius. It uses the same convergence test and has no time cap. The 3-D field is then restored and the memory is kept. This phase is cheap, because no element is on the 3-D path. It is independent of equil_time_max.

The rate of each pass is measured over exactly that pass’s memory advance. The criterion is a global mean. It bounds the mean bed velocity, not the velocity at every point, and it is not a measure of how far the relaxation has gone. The default equil_rate_tol stops the spin-up when the bed moves slower than \(10^{-3}\) m/yr. In a test with a held polar cap relaxed over 500 kyr, this is reached at about 83 % of the full relaxation. Full relaxation over such spans is not affordable in realistic cases, so the spin-up gives a practical reference, not a fully relaxed one. For a reproducible reference, fix the length of the spin-up with equil_time_max and set equil_rate_tol = 0, as the reference of the VILMA1 versus VILMA2 deglaciation does. Elements with very high viscosity do not equilibrate within any practical cap, which is what the lid rule addresses. test_spinup asserts that the spin-up relaxes the held load well beyond a single cold step, and that the state after it is near-stationary. The spin-up is not available with solver = "v1".
A zero-length update (dt = 0) advances neither time nor memory. It solves the sea-level equation under the ice it is handed, against the current memory, and refreshes the surface fields, so relative sea level, the ocean function and h_ice describe the same ice. It is idempotent: a second call with the same ice changes nothing. The spin-up begins with one, and a run without spin-up (a restarted run included) begins with one, to seed the start-slice ice. A negative dt stops the run.






TipWhere this lives in the code



vilma_viscoelastic (1D stepper + shared kernel), vilma_response (ve_response field driver, begin_step/commit_step), vilma_io (netCDF restart), and vilma_coupling (host init/update contract, spin-up), vilma_timestep (the sub-step controller) and vilma_sle (the load–memory iteration). The cost of the drift solve in begin_step is addressed in Solver.

title: Toroidal flow under lateral viscosity
text: A surface load on a radially symmetric Earth drives only spheroidal deformation: radial and consoidal displacement, \(U\) and \(V\). Once viscosity varies laterally this is no longer true. The Maxwell relaxation then also drives toroidal flow \(W\): horizontal, divergence-free motion with no radial component. That flow feeds back into the spheroidal field. VILMA2 carries this toroidal degree of freedom in its 3D path, as VILMA1 does.

title: Toroidal flow under lateral viscosity
section: Why lateral viscosity drives toroidal flow
text:
Why lateral viscosity drives toroidal flow
The displacement is expanded in vector spherical harmonics (see Spectral reduction),
\[
\mathbf{u} = \sum_{jm}\Bigl[\,U_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(-1)}_{jm}
+ V_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(1)}_{jm}
+ W_{jm}(r)\,\mathbf{S}^{(0)}_{jm}\,\Bigr],
\qquad
\mathbf{S}^{(0)}_{jm} = \mathbf{e}_r\times\nabla_1 Y_{jm},
\]
and the strain and memory stress are expanded in the six tensor spherical harmonics \(Z^{(\lambda)}_{jm}\), \(\lambda = 1,\dots,6\) (Martinec 2000, App. B). The spheroidal field lives in \(\lambda\in\{1,2,5,6\}\) and the toroidal field in \(\lambda\in\{3,4\}\).
On a radially symmetric Earth the two families are decoupled:

the left-hand-side operator has no term coupling \(W\) to \(U\), \(V\), \(F\) or \(\Pi\) (no pressure, self-gravity or mixed shear contribution);
the surface forcing has no \(\delta W\) term (Martinec 2000, eq. 84), so a load never forces \(W\) directly;
with \(M = \mu\Delta t/\eta(r)\) the memory update is diagonal in \(\lambda\), so a spheroidal memory stays spheroidal.

\(W\) is therefore identically zero, and the solver needs only the four spheroidal channels. With a laterally varying \(\eta(\theta,\varphi)\) the third point fails. The memory update \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{+} = (1-M)\,\boldsymbol{\tau} -
2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) multiplies the stress by a field \(M(\theta,\varphi)\) pointwise. That product mixes all six tensor components. As Martinec (2000) notes after eq. (110), lateral viscosity removes both the decoupling and the degeneracy of the spheroidal and toroidal displacements. The loop closes in three steps:

The spheroidal memory, multiplied by \(M(\theta,\varphi)\), acquires \(\lambda = 3,4\) components.
These force \(W\) through the dissipative right-hand side.
The toroidal strain of \(W\), multiplied again by \(M(\theta,\varphi)\), feeds back into \(\lambda \in \{1,2,5,6\}\) and hence into uplift and geoid.

Perturbation reasoning predicts \(W\) at first order in the lateral viscosity contrast and its feedback on uplift at second order, which the tests confirm.






TipWhen is W exactly zero?



Toroidal flow vanishes for axisymmetric configurations (load and viscosity symmetric about a common axis), not for every configuration with a shared mirror plane. Under a reflection the toroidal potential is odd. A \(Y_{20}\) load over a \(\cos 2\varphi\) viscosity pattern is mirror-symmetric, yet drives \(W \propto \sin 2\varphi\).

title: Toroidal flow under lateral viscosity
text:
Toroidal strain and memory
For \(\mathbf{u} = W(r)\,\mathbf{e}_r\times\nabla_1 Y_{jm}\) the strain is
\[
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} =
\Bigl(W' - \frac{W}{r}\Bigr) Z^{(3)}_{jm} + \frac{W}{r}\,Z^{(4)}_{jm},
\]
with the dyadic forms (Martinec 2000, B10–B11, in terms of the angular functions \(E,F,G,H\))
\[
Z^{(3)} = -F\,\mathbf{e}_{r\theta} + E\,\mathbf{e}_{r\varphi},
\qquad
Z^{(4)} = G\,\mathbf{e}_{\theta\varphi} - H\,(\mathbf{e}_{\theta\theta} - \mathbf{e}_{\varphi\varphi}),
\]
the toroidal companions of \(Z^{(2)}\) and \(Z^{(6)}\). Their norms (B13) are
\[
\lVert Z^{(3)}\rVert^2 = \tfrac{J}{2},
\qquad
\lVert Z^{(4)}\rVert^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}J(J-2),
\qquad J = j(j+1).
\]
On the P1 radial elements, with \(W = W^k\psi_k + W^{k+1}\psi_{k+1}\) and \(\varepsilon = a/h + b\,\psi_k/r + c\,\psi_{k+1}/r\) (Martinec 2000, eqs. 87–88), the two strain rows the spheroidal kernel omits are



\(\lambda\)
\(a\)
\(b\)
\(c\)




3
\(W^{k+1} - W^k\)
\(-W^k\)
\(-W^{k+1}\)


4
\(0\)

\(W^{k+1}\)



The strain map is block-diagonal: \(\lambda = 3,4\) depend only on \(W\) and \(\lambda \in \{1,2,5,6\}\) only on \(U,V\). The toroidal memory is therefore carried as two extra channels of the same memory arrays (channels 5 and 6), and the spheroidal and toroidal kernels are independent. At degree 1, \(Z^{(4)}_{1m}\equiv 0\) (\(J = 2\)), so the \(\lambda = 4\) slot carries no memory there, as for \(\lambda = 6\).

title: Toroidal flow under lateral viscosity
text:
The toroidal operator
The toroidal part of the shear energy (Martinec 2000, eq. 80) is
\[
2\!\int\!\mu\,\Bigl[\lVert Z^{(3)}\rVert^2\,\varepsilon^{3}\,\delta\varepsilon^{3}
+ \lVert Z^{(4)}\rVert^2\,\varepsilon^{4}\,\delta\varepsilon^{4}\Bigr] r^2\,\mathrm{d}r,
\]
which per element \(k\) discretizes to
\[
\mu_k\Bigl\{ J\bigl[I^1_{\alpha\beta} - I^3_{\beta\alpha} - I^3_{\alpha\beta} + I^6_{\alpha\beta}\bigr]
+ J(J-2)\,I^6_{\alpha\beta}\Bigr\}\,W^\alpha\,\delta W^\beta,
\]
using the same Appendix-C integrals as the spheroidal block. No density, gravity or pressure enters. Rather than adding \(W\) as a fifth interleaved field to the spheroidal system, VILMA2 gives it its own per-degree operator. That operator is symmetric and tridiagonal, and it is factored once per degree and reused for all orders, loads and steps, like the spheroidal one (see Solver). The spheroidal operator is untouched.
Two conditions make it non-singular:

Fluid regions. Where \(\mu = 0\) (the inviscid core) there is no shear energy and \(W\) has no stiffness. These nodes are pinned, \(W = 0\). This is a Dirichlet condition on a degree of freedom the fluid does not have.
Degree 1. At \(j = 1\) a rigid rotation, \(W \propto r\), has no strain and is a null mode. It is removed by one KKT border row per solid shell, \(\sum_k W^k\!\int\!\psi_k\,r^3\,\mathrm{d}r = 0\), which states \(\int\mathbf{x}\times\mathbf{u}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\) (no net rotation) for that shell. A structure with a solid inner core has two such shells. This is a gauge: a rigid rotation moves no output.

title: Toroidal flow under lateral viscosity
text:
Coupling into the time step
Because the surface load never forces \(W\), the toroidal field has no elastic gain. It is pure relaxation drift. Within the field driver a step proceeds as follows:

begin_step solves, for every \((j,m)\), the spheroidal drift and the toroidal drift \(W\) from the dissipative forcing of the current memory, the latter with the toroidal operator.
The SLE fixed point calls apply() as usual. \(W\) does not enter uplift or geoid directly, so the affine structure is unchanged.
The memory advance follows. In each genuinely 3-D element all six dyadic components of memory and strain, spheroidal and toroidal, are synthesized on the Gauss grid and multiplied pointwise by \(M(\theta,\varphi)\). The increment is analysed back into all six channels. This is where the two families exchange stress. Laterally uniform elements advance their toroidal channels on the per-degree spectral path, where they simply relax.

The toroidal channels are switched on only when some element is genuinely 3-D (its lateral \(\log_{10}\eta\) spread exceeds visc_3d_tol) and l_toroidal = .true.. The memory arrays then widen from four to six channels (about 50 % more memory state). A radially symmetric or laterally uniform run keeps four channels and pays nothing. Once on, the channels stay on for the rest of the run: a later laterally uniform field no longer drives \(W\), but existing toroidal memory must still relax.
Restart files record the channel count. A spheroidal (four-channel) restart can be read into a toroidal run, with the toroidal memory starting at zero. Reading a toroidal restart into a spheroidal run is an error, since it would discard memory.

title: Governing equations
text: VILMA2 solves the equations of a self-gravitating, incompressible, Maxwell-viscoelastic sphere \(\mathcal{B}\) of radius \(a\) subject to a surface mass load. The formulation is the incremental, quasi-static field theory of Martinec (2000); the equation numbers in this section refer to that paper.

title: Governing equations
text:
Incremental field equations
We work with the incremental (perturbation) fields superimposed on a hydrostatic reference state with density \(\rho_0(r)\) and gravity \(g_0(r)\). The unknowns are the displacement \(\mathbf{u}\), the incremental gravitational potential \(\varphi_1\), and the incompressibility pressure (Lagrange multiplier) \(\Pi\).

Momentum balance
In the quasi-static limit the linearized, pre-stressed momentum balance reads (Martinec 2000, eq. 1)
\[
\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol{\tau}
\;-\; \rho_0\,\nabla\varphi_1
\;+\; \operatorname{div}(\rho_0\mathbf{u})\,\nabla\varphi_0
\;-\; \nabla\!\left(\rho_0\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\varphi_0\right)
\;=\; \mathbf{0},
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is the incremental (Cauchy) stress and \(\varphi_0\) the reference potential (\(\nabla\varphi_0 = \mathbf{g}_0\)). The last three terms are the self-gravity body force: the perturbed-potential gradient \(-\rho_0\nabla\varphi_1\), the advected-density buoyancy \(\operatorname{div}(\rho_0\mathbf{u})\,\nabla\varphi_0\), and the material/pre-stress advection term. These couple deformation to gravity and are the reason GIA is a global, self-gravitating problem rather than a local flexure problem.


Poisson equation
The incremental potential is sourced by the advected density via Poisson’s equation (eq. 2),
\[
\nabla^2\varphi_1 \;+\; 4\pi G \,\operatorname{div}(\rho_0\mathbf{u}) \;=\; 0,
\qquad
\rho_1 = -\operatorname{div}(\rho_0\mathbf{u}),
\]
valid throughout the interior. Outside the body \(\varphi_1\) is harmonic and decays as \(r^{-(\ell+1)}\) for each degree \(\ell\); this exterior matching becomes a boundary condition at the surface (see Radial finite elements). The applied surface load contributes its own Newtonian potential, which enters \(\varphi_1\) through the surface forcing.


Constitutive law
The stress splits into an isotropic part carried by the pressure and a deviatoric part carried by shear:
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau} \;=\; \Pi\,\mathbf{I} \;+\; 2\mu\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{dev}},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\nabla\mathbf{u} + \nabla\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}\right).
\]
For the elastic problem this is Hooke’s law with shear modulus \(\mu(r)\). For the viscoelastic Maxwell body the deviatoric stress acquires a relaxing memory term, described in Rheology. The bulk response is taken incompressible (\(K\to\infty\)), so \(\Pi\) is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing the kinematic constraint below rather than a state variable.


Incompressibility
\[
\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u} \;=\; 0 \qquad\text{(eq. 5).}
\]
Incompressibility is the standard idealization for mantle GIA on glacial timescales: it removes the seismic compressional modes (irrelevant here), simplifies the rheology to a single shear modulus, and makes the degree-0 (radial breathing) displacement vanish identically.

title: Governing equations
text:
Reference structure
The reference state is a layered, spherically symmetric model. Within each layer the density \(\rho_k\) and shear modulus \(\mu_k\) are piecewise constant, and the reference gravity follows from the enclosed mass,
\[
g_0(r) = \frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho_k\, r + \frac{R_k}{r^2}\right),
\qquad
R_k = \sum_{i\le k}(\rho_{i-1}-\rho_i)\,r_i^{3},
\quad R_1 = 0,
\]
(Martinec 2000, eqs. 76–77). The inviscid fluid core is meshed explicitly with \(\mu = 0\), so free-slip at the core–mantle boundary emerges from the weak form rather than being imposed as an explicit boundary condition. The elastic lithosphere is the \(\eta\to\infty\) limit of the Maxwell layers (taken exactly, never large-but-finite — a finite value would inject a spurious slow relaxation mode).
The benchmark earth model used throughout validation is M3–L70–V01 (70 km elastic lithosphere, three viscous mantle layers, inviscid core), the incompressible model of the Charles University GIA benchmark (Spada et al. 2011).

title: Governing equations
text:
Weak (energy) form
Rather than discretizing the strong PDEs directly, the solver discretizes the second variation of an energy functional — this is what guarantees a symmetric operator. One seeks \((\mathbf{u},\varphi_1,\Pi)\) such that \(\delta E = \delta F\) for all admissible test functions (Martinec 2000, eq. 47), with
\[
E = E_{\text{press}} + E_{\text{shear}} + E_{\text{grav}} + E_{\text{uniq}},
\]








Term
Expression (schematic)
Role




\(E_{\text{press}}\)
\(\displaystyle\int \Pi\,\operatorname{div}\mathbf{u}\,\mathrm{d}V\)
couples pressure \(\leftrightarrow\) incompressibility


\(E_{\text{shear}}\)
\(\displaystyle\int \mu\,(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\!:\!\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}V\)
elastic shear energy


\(E_{\text{grav}}\)
self-gravity body force \(+\ \tfrac{1}{8\pi G}\!\int|\nabla\varphi_1|^2\)
gravitational coupling


\(E_{\text{uniq}}\)
rigid-mode penalty
removes translation/rotation null space — degree 1 only



and surface forcing \(F_{\text{surf}} = \int_{\partial\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{b}_0\cdot\mathbf{u} + b_1\varphi_1)\,\mathrm{d}S\) with \(\mathbf{b}_0 = -g_0(a)\,\sigma\,\mathbf{e}_r\) (eqs. 36–38). The viscoelastic problem adds a dissipative forcing \(F_{\text{diss}}\) built from the memory stress (see Rheology).
Because the discrete operator is the Hessian of this functional, it is symmetric by construction. Enforcing that symmetry term-by-term was, in practice, the key to getting the low-degree elastic Love numbers right — see the Love-numbers benchmark.

title: Governing equations
text:
Conventions and constants

Densities: the rho_ice, rho_water parameters (&vilma; a host sets its own pair, used throughout), by default \(\rho_{\text{ice}} = 917\), \(\rho_{\text{water}} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) (the GIA benchmarks use \(\rho_{\text{ice}} = 931\), set by the benchmark tests); surface gravity \(g_0 = 9.815\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Mass — not volume — is conserved, applying \(\rho_{\text{ice}}/\rho_{\text{water}}\) exactly once in each of the flotation criterion, the eustatic conversion, and the sea-level equation.
Degree 1 is frame-dependent. The geocenter (degree-1) signal is physical and is not hard-coded. By default displacement and geoid are both expressed in the centre-of-mass (CM) frame (Blewitt 2003) (deg1_frame = "cm"). See Sea-level equation and Radial finite elements.







TipWhere this lives in the code



The governing equations are realized in vilma_earth_structure (reference layers and gravity), vilma_radial_fe (the assembled energy-Hessian operator), and vilma_viscoelastic (the Maxwell memory term). The continuous-to-discrete mapping is documented term-by-term in the repository’s doc/formulation.md.

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
text: The mantle is modelled as an incompressible Maxwell body: it responds elastically on short timescales and viscously on long ones, with a single Maxwell time \(\tau_M = \eta/\mu\) per layer. VILMA2 integrates this constitutive law explicitly in the time domain — there is no normal-mode decomposition and no Laplace transform. This is the structural choice that admits laterally varying (3D) viscosity without changing the operator. The extra cost of a 3D run lies in the memory advance, and in the shorter time step that low viscosities require.

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
text:
The Maxwell body
For a deviatoric stress \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) and deviatoric strain \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\), the Maxwell rheology is
\[
\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}} + \frac{\mu}{\eta}\,\boldsymbol{\tau}
\;=\; 2\mu\,\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}},
\]
with \(\mu(r)\) the shear modulus and \(\eta(r)\) the viscosity. Two limits are exact and are used as validation anchors:

Elastic / lithosphere: \(\eta\to\infty \Rightarrow\) Hooke’s law \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = 2\mu\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\). The lithosphere is taken as \(\eta = \infty\) exactly; a large-but-finite value would seed a spurious slow mode that contaminates multi-cycle runs.
Fluid / inviscid core: \(\mu\to 0 \Rightarrow\) the layer carries no deviatoric stress (free-slip).

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
text:
Explicit memory-stress scheme
Following Martinec (2000) (§3, eqs. 23–25), the total stress at time step \(i\) is the instantaneous elastic stress — computed by the same elastic operator every step — plus a memory stress \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V}\) that encodes the relaxation history:
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i}
\;=\; (1 - M)\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1}
\;-\; 2\mu\,M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\,i},
\qquad
M \equiv \frac{\mu\,\Delta t}{\eta}.
\]
This is the \(\omega = 1\) (fully explicit) update. The memory stress enters the right-hand side of the field equations as a dissipative forcing
\[
F_{\text{diss}} \;=\; -\!\int \boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} : \delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\ \mathrm{d}V
\qquad\text{(eq. 35).}
\]
The crucial consequence: the left-hand-side operator never changes in time. It is assembled, equilibrated, and LU-factored once, then reused at every step with a fresh right-hand side. Each step costs a back-substitution, not a re-factorization (see Solver). The time step enters only through \(M\), so changing \(\Delta t\) is a rescale, never a re-factorization.

Memory time schemes
The memory update is selected by scheme. All schemes share the fixed operator; they differ only in how \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V}\) is advanced over a step.









scheme
Update
Order, stability
Step control




"fe" (default)
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} = (1-M)\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1} - 2\mu M\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i}\)
1st order, conditionally stable
equal sub-steps with \(M \le\) cfl


"trap"
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i} = \dfrac{(1-M/2)\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i-1} - \mu M\,(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i-1}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i})}{1+M/2}\)
2nd order, A-stable (Crank–Nicolson)
adaptive, step-doubling error estimate



"fe" is the \(\omega = 1\) scheme of Martinec (2000) and matches how VILMA1 marches its memory. "trap" is implicit in the end-of-step strain \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{i}\), which itself depends on \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{V,i}\). The step endpoint is therefore iterated to a consistent strain–memory pair. In the coupled model this iteration runs inside the sea-level solve, so the ocean load converges together with the memory. It stops when the surface drift changes by less than \(10^{-6}\) (relative) between passes, or after sle_max_mem_iter passes (default 20).
scheme takes "fe" or "trap"; any other value stops the run. The exponential (ETD1) and backward-Euler updates exist only in the single-degree stepper (ve_degree), as controls for the convergence tests (test_etd1, test_couple_order); they are not settings of the model.






NoteWhy explicit, not implicit or normal-mode



With the explicit update, the memory stress at step \(i\) depends only on the previous step’s stress and strain — both known. Nothing in the operator depends on viscosity, so a spatially varying \(\eta(r,\theta,\phi)\) changes only the scalar \(M\) that multiplies known fields pointwise. The angular harmonics stay decoupled in the solve. A normal-mode method, by contrast, must re-solve a degree-by-degree eigenvalue problem whenever the radial structure changes and cannot represent lateral viscosity at all without abandoning the mode basis.

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
section: From layers to the same kernel in 1D and 3D
text:
From layers to the same kernel in 1D and 3D
In the 1D (radially symmetric) case the memory stress evolves directly on the tensor spherical-harmonic coefficients (Martinec 2000, §9): there is no spatial grid. Per radial element it is stored for the four spheroidal tensor components \(\lambda\in\{1,2,5,6\}\) (eq. 109), and the strain coefficients follow from the nodal radial functions \(U,V\) via eq. 87–88. The dissipative right-hand side is a two-point radial Gauss quadrature of the spectral double-dot \(\sum_\lambda \lVert Z^\lambda\rVert^2\,\tau^{V,\lambda}\,\delta\varepsilon^\lambda\) with the component norms \(\{1,\ J/2,\ 2J^2,\ 2J(J-2)\}\), \(J = \ell(\ell+1)\) (eqs. 110, B13).
With laterally varying viscosity the pointwise product \(M(\theta,\varphi)\,\tau\) mixes spheroidal and toroidal stress. The toroidal components \(\lambda\in\{3,4\}\) (norms \(J/2\), \(J(J-2)/2\)) can then be carried as well (l_toroidal), and the toroidal displacement \(W\) they force feeds back into the spheroidal field. See Toroidal flow.
In the 3D (laterally varying viscosity) case the operator, the strain coefficients and the dissipative right-hand side are unchanged; only the memory advance differs. \(M = \mu\Delta t/\eta(\theta,\varphi)\) becomes a field, so for each radial element the memory and strain tensors are synthesized on the Gauss–Legendre grid from their six dyadic components (Martinec 2000, B10–B11), advanced pointwise, and analysed back to spectral space (pseudo-spectral). The per-element Maxwell routines (strain_coeffs, ve_strain_constants, dissipative_rhs, advance_memory) are shared verbatim between the 1D stepper and the field driver. There is no duplicated algorithm and no separate “3D solver”.
Three details matter in practice:

Only genuinely 3-D elements pay for the grid round trip. An element is treated as 3-D when its lateral spread of \(\log_{10}\eta\) exceeds visc_3d_tol (default \(10^{-3}\) dex). Every other Maxwell element collapses to its lateral-mean rate and advances on the cheap per-degree spectral path, as in VILMA1’s 1-D/3-D layer split. A laterally uniform field therefore flags no element as 3-D and costs exactly the 1D run.
The update is analysed as an increment. The grid step is written \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{+} = \boldsymbol{\tau} - M(\boldsymbol{\tau} + 2\mu\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\), and only the increment is transformed back. Analysing \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{+}\) itself would put the transform’s round-off (\(\sim 10^{-13}\) relative to \(|\boldsymbol{\tau}|\)) on a change of size \(M|\boldsymbol{\tau}|\). For the stiffest Maxwell elements (\(M\sim10^{-10}\) at \(\eta\sim10^{30}\) Pa s) that error is of order one per step.
Elastic and fluid layers stay memory-free. A 3-D field modulates only the Maxwell layers of the earth model. A layer declared elastic (rheology = 0) stays exactly elastic and laterally uniform, whatever the file prescribes there. The same holds for a fluid layer. The lid rule below is a separate, optional rule that acts on Maxwell elements.


The 3-D viscosity input chain
With l_visc_3d = .true. the lateral field is built once at initialization, in a fixed order. Each stage acts on the result of the previous one.

Read. visc_3d_file holds absolute \(\log_{10}\eta\) [Pa s]. With visc_3d_structure = 0 it is a field on (lon, lat, r), the radius in meters, with the variable names name_visc, name_visc_lon, name_visc_lat and name_visc_r. With visc_3d_structure \(\ge 1\) the file is in the FesmData layout, log10_visc(lon, lat, depth, structure), with depth in meters below a surface radius of 6371 km. The value is then the index of the structure to read, and the name_visc* names are ignored. The default is the Bagge et al. (2021) field of the FesmData product GLOBAL-T170_SolidEarth-Bagge2021.nc, structure 6 (v_1.0_s16). The field is interpolated in \(\log_{10}\eta\) onto the Gauss grid and the radial nodes: bilinear in longitude (periodic) and latitude, linear in radius. Outside the latitude or radius range of the file the nearest value is used. An axis may be stored in either direction. A non-monotonic axis stops the run.
Perturb (f_visc_sd, default 0). The field is shifted by f_visc_sd standard deviations, for uncertainty ensembles. The standard deviation is read from the variable name_visc_sd if one is named (lon-lat-r layout only). Otherwise it is relative, f_visc_rel \(\times\,\lvert\log_{10}\eta\rvert\) (default 0.1).
Shift (visc_shift_file, default "", none). The file holds a shift dlog10_visc(lon, lat, r) in dex, with the fixed names lon, lat and r (radius in meters). It is read and interpolated as the field itself and added to it. This changes viscosity by region and depth, for example per ensemble member. Outside the radial range of the file the shift is zero, so a file that covers only the upper mantle shifts only the upper mantle. A NaN, Inf or fill value in the viscosity, its standard deviation or the shift stops the run, naming the file and variable. visc_shift_file needs l_visc_3d = .true.; the run stops otherwise.
Clamp to [visc_log10_min, visc_log10_max] (defaults 19.5 and 30.0). The floor bounds the fastest relaxation and so the time step (see Stability).
Lid rule (visc_3d_lid_depth, default 0, off). The nodal field is first averaged to the radial elements (the mean of \(\log_{10}\eta\) at the two nodes). In a Maxwell element that lies wholly above visc_3d_lid_depth [m], every grid point whose \(\log_{10}\eta\) exceeds visc_3d_lid_log10max (default 22.0) is then set to visc_log10_max. Such points relax over millions of years, so a held-load spin-up never equilibrates them. The rule splits the lid into points that relax within thousands of years and points that do not relax on the run’s time scale. The capped points still carry memory, so they are close to elastic, not exactly elastic. The rule acts on elements, not nodes, because a node at the lid base is shared with the element below. test_visc_lid asserts that only lid elements above the threshold change.
1-D/3-D split (visc_3d_tol, default \(10^{-3}\) dex). Elements whose lateral spread exceeds the tolerance run on the 3-D path, as described above. A larger tolerance moves weakly varying elements to the 1-D path. This lowers the cost of the memory advance and approximates their lateral structure by its mean.

The rotation channels relax on the radial profile of the field that results from this chain.

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
text:
Stability
The explicit scheme is conditionally stable: \(|1-M| < 1\) bounds the step by the shortest Maxwell time present,
\[
\Delta t \;<\; \frac{2\,\eta_{\min}}{\mu}.
\]
The "fe" stepper keeps a factor-2 margin: it splits each coupling interval into equal sub-steps with \(M \le\) cfl (default 1). A guard rolls a sub-step back and halves it if the memory norm grows abnormally; it normally never fires. A viscosity floor (visc_log10_min, default \(10^{19.5}\) Pa s) caps the fastest relaxation of a 3-D field and so sets a usable step. "trap" is A-stable and chooses its step by accuracy alone. Elastic layers (\(M\to 0\)) freeze and carry no memory; fluid layers (\(\mu = 0\)) carry no memory either.






TipWhere this lives in the code



vilma_viscoelastic holds both the 1D per-degree stepper (ve_degree) and the shared per-element kernel. vilma_earth_structure (load_visc_3d) and vilma_response build the 3-D field. The memory stress is the largest part of the state that a restart carries, but not all of it: see Memory storage and restart. Time integration is validated by test_relax (a held load relaxes elastic \(\to\) fluid, \(t_{\text{relax}}\propto\eta\), step-converged) and is benchmarked in Sea-level equation.
crumbs: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress

title: Maxwell rheology and the memory stress
text:
A modal reduction was tried
For an incompressible layered Maxwell Earth the per-degree response is a finite sum of exponential relaxation modes, with only a handful of modes dominating the surface response at each degree. This suggests a natural reduction: replace the full radial memory tensor by \(K\) scalar amplitudes \(\xi_k(\ell,m)\) per coefficient, each advancing by its exact exponential. Radially varying viscosity is then exact in the limit \(K \to \infty\), and lateral viscosity is folded in as a rate modulation of each mode by the local viscosity in the depth band that mode samples.
We implemented and validated such a reduced solver, but decided against retaining it. The measured speed-up over the full explicit scheme was modest, and the approximation error grew rapidly once lateral viscosity contrasts or strongly time-varying loads were introduced. Since the explicit memory-stress scheme is already cheap — one back-substitution per step, with no angular coupling — the added complexity of maintaining a second response operator was not justified. The full solver is retained as the single response path, and the reduced solver has been removed from the code; it survives in the git history up to commit cbf77bd.

title: Implementation and attribution
text: VILMA2 is a modern-Fortran implementation of published GIA physics, built on a small set of well-established numerical libraries. This page records what the model is built on, and what informed its development and validation.

title: Implementation and attribution
text:
Physics and references
VILMA2 reproduces the physics of VILMA1: an incompressible, self-gravitating, Maxwell-viscoelastic sphere with rotational feedback and a full migrating-coastline sea-level equation. VILMA1’s character is documented in Albrecht et al. (2024) and Bagge et al. (2021). The numerical method follows Martinec (2000), with rotation from Martinec and Hagedoorn (2014) and the sea-level equation from Kendall et al. (2005) and Martinec et al. (2018).
The implementation is modern and minimal: a small, dependency-light Fortran codebase organized as single-purpose modules (vilma_*), validated rung-by-rung against the community benchmarks. It is 3D-ready from the start: laterally varying viscosity leaves the per-degree operator and its factorization unchanged. The extra cost of a 3D run lies in the memory advance (see Rheology).

title: Implementation and attribution
text:
Libraries we build on



Library
Role
Reference




SHTns
fast spherical-harmonic transforms (forward/inverse, quadrature, point & gradient evaluation)
Schaeffer (2013)


FFTW3
the longitudinal FFTs underlying SHTns
Frigo and Johnson (2005)


netCDF
restart and output I/O
—


fesm-utils
shared build system + helper library (ncio, namelists, lon-lat grids), and the builds of FFTW and SHTns
—



The FFT and spherical-harmonic transform are central, not incidental. A pseudo-spectral method moves between grid and spectral space many times per step: the SLE forms its ocean-function product on the grid and its load–response convolution in spectral space. Using SHTns and FFTW for that kernel, rather than a hand-rolled transform, keeps the model fast at the resolutions of interest. The transform convention (orthonormal, no Condon–Shortley phase, Gauss grid) is pinned across the whole code. See Spectral reduction.
The linear solver, by contrast, is hand-rolled: a dependency-free, re-entrant, pivoted banded LU (vilma_band). This choice avoids an external dependency that would complicate linking into an OpenMP host. Neither LIS, which an early version used, nor LAPACK is linked. See Solver.

title: Implementation and attribution
section: Codebases and datasets that informed the validation
text:
Codebases and datasets that informed the validation
Several existing codebases provided independent reference solutions and datasets used during validation of VILMA2. Each implements the physics in a somewhat different way, which was helpful for understanding the method, and each supplied reference data used in the benchmark pages:

giapy (S. B. Kachuck, MIT) — source of the vendored M3–L70–V01 Love-number table, the SBK sea-level reference curves, and the analytic load/basin specifications for the Martinec et al. (2018) cases.
TABOO (D. Melini, GPLv3) — a normal-mode code used as an independent reference to regenerate the M3–L70–V01 Love numbers (NV=3, CODE=7).
isostasy_data / FastIsostasy.jl (J. Jereczek) — source of the Spada et al. (2011) disc-load spatial-response reference.

Full provenance and licensing of every vendored dataset is in the repository’s data/benchmarks/PROVENANCE.md.

title: Implementation and attribution
text:
Build and host coupling
The model uses a configme build: a machine fragment inserted into a Makefile template. Dependencies are provided through a fesm-utils checkout (FFTW, SHTns) plus system netCDF, and runs are staged with runme. Both are covered in Install & run.
The host-coupling contract, designed for CLIMBER-X, is intentionally narrow. The host passes ice thickness in and receives relative sea level and bedrock out, on its own grid. It can also read the two parts of relative sea level (bed change and sea-surface change), the ocean function and the barystatic scalars. The model owns its Gauss grid and the host↔︎Gauss remap (conservative in, bilinear out), built from the parameter record, and keeps all spherical-harmonic transforms inside. A host that resolves the ice margin on its own grid can pass host-resolved terms as well.

title: Implementation and attribution
text:
License and citation
See the repository for the current license. When citing the method, cite the primary sources — above all Martinec (2000) for the spectral–finite-element approach, and Spada et al. (2011) and Martinec et al. (2018) for the benchmarks against which VILMA2 is validated.

title: Benchmark: low-viscosity zone (lateral viscosity)
text:
Reference: Weerdesteijn et al. (2023), section 5.2, the short-timescale low-viscosity-region case computed with ASPECT, Abaqus and TABOO (Weerdesteijn et al. 2023). Test: test_benchmark_lvz (in make check-slow). Asserted: vertical displacement at the load center after 200 yr within 8 % of the published values, without and with the low-viscosity zone. Measured (ifx, albedo): 2.6 % and 1.0 %.
This benchmark tests the laterally varying viscosity against published results of three-dimensional finite-element codes. It is the only test of the 3-D path against codes other than VILMA1.

title: Benchmark: low-viscosity zone (lateral viscosity)
text:
Load and setup

Earth model M3–L70–V01.
An axisymmetric ice disc of 100 km radius (\(\rho_\text{ice} = 931\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)). Its height grows linearly from 0 to 100 m over 100 yr and is then held to 200 yr.
A cylindrical low-viscosity zone (LVZ) under the load: radius 100 km, depth 70–170 km, viscosity \(10^{19}\) Pa s in an upper mantle of \(10^{21}\) Pa s. The shear modulus is unchanged.
Two runs: the homogeneous model (no LVZ) and the model with the LVZ.

The load and the LVZ are axisymmetric, so the problem has order \(m = 0\) only. The test runs with mmax = 0 at \(\ell_\max = 512\) (a shortest half-wavelength of about 40 km, against the 100 km radius of the disc) with a step of 2.5 yr. It drives the viscoelastic response with the ice load directly. There is no ocean and no sea-level equation.

title: Benchmark: low-viscosity zone (lateral viscosity)
text:
Reference data and metrics
The reference values are the vertical surface displacement at the load center at \(t = 200\) yr: \(-0.75\) m for the homogeneous model and \(-1.23\) m with the LVZ. The published codes differ among themselves. ASPECT and Abaqus agree to 1–3 %. ASPECT, which has no self-gravity, and TABOO, which has, agree to 0.3 % at the load center of the homogeneous model. Self-gravity is thus a sub-percent effect in this case, and the published numbers are a valid reference for a self-gravitating spherical model to within a few percent. The tolerance of the test is 8 %.

Reference: Spada et al. (2011), test 3/2, Table 14, earth model M3–L70–V01 (Spada et al. 2011). Test: test_rotation (in make check). Asserted: rigid inertia within 2 % of the published geometrical factor; polar motion \(|m(t)|\) within 3 % at 0, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 kyr, for a cap and a disc load. Measured (ifx, albedo): inertia 0.09 % and 0.41 %; polar motion within 0.4 % (cap) and 0.9 % (disc).
This benchmark tests the rotational feedback: the polar motion excited by a surface load on a viscoelastic Earth, from the quasi-static Liouville equation (see Rotational feedback).

title: Benchmark: rotation (polar motion)
text:
Load and setup

Two axisymmetric ice loads of 10° radius centered at colatitude 25°, longitude 75°: a cap of 1500 m and a disc of 1000 m (\(\rho_\text{ice} = 931\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)), applied as a Heaviside load and held for 20 kyr.
Earth model M3–L70–V01, \(C - A = 2.63\times10^{35}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\).
Grid \(\ell_\max = 128\), step 25 yr. There is no ocean load: the test drives the rotation module directly with the ice load.

title: Benchmark: rotation (polar motion)
text:
Reference data and metrics
The reference is Table 14 of Spada et al. (2011), the modulus of polar motion \(|m|\) in degrees at six times. The table has two cases. The model integrates the quasi-static Liouville equation, in which the Chandler wobble is neglected, so the comparison uses the column with the Chandler wobble excluded (\(C_w = 0\)). The values are those of the normal-mode code TABOO. They are tabulated to three significant digits, which limits the comparison to about 0.4 %. VILMA1 did not contribute polar motion to this test.
The test makes three checks.

Normalization. The rigid (2,1) inertia of each load, divided by \(C - A\), reproduces the published geometrical factor \(G\) (Spada eq. 31). This isolates the mapping from the load to the inertia tensor from the viscoelastic response.
Love numbers. The elastic tidal number \(k^T_e\) and the secular number \(k_s\) lie in the physical range (\(0 < k^T_e < k_s\), \(0.5 < k_s < 1.5\)).
Polar motion. \(|m(t)|\) at the six tabulated times.

title: Benchmark: disc-load response
text:
Reference: Spada et al. (2011), disc-load test, earth model M3–L70–V01 (Spada et al. 2011). Test: test_benchmark_disc (in make check). Asserted: elastic profile within 6 % (uplift) and 4 % (geoid) of the peak, away from the disc edge; center uplift within 3 % at 1, 2, 5 and 10 kyr. Measured (ifx, albedo): 4.0 % and 2.8 % for the elastic profile; 0.02–0.6 % for the center uplift.
This benchmark integrates the per-degree response over a spatial load and adds the time relaxation, testing the spatial synthesis and the Maxwell stepper together against a spatial reference.

title: Benchmark: disc-load response
text:
Load and setup

A 10° radius disc of 1000 m ice (\(\rho_{\text{ice}} = 931\
\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)) on elevated bedrock — no ocean load.
Earth model M3–L70–V01 (as for the Love numbers).
The disc is expanded in Legendre coefficients \(\sigma_n = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\,[P_{n-1}-P_{n+1}]\) and the spatial response is synthesized as \(u(\theta) = \sum_n U_n(a)\,\sigma_n\,P_n(\cos\theta)\).

title: Benchmark: disc-load response
text:
Reference data and metrics
The reference is the spatial response at colatitudes \(\theta = 0\):\(0.1\):\(20°\) (201 points) and times \(t = [0,1,2,5,10,100]\) kyr (column 1, \(t=0\), is the elastic response). The reference provides three fields: vertical displacement \(u\), geoid \(n\), and uplift rate \(\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}t\). The stored curves are piecewise linear on a 1° grid, which limits how closely any smooth solution can match them (see data/benchmarks/PROVENANCE.md).
The test makes two comparisons.

Elastic profile. \(u(\theta)\) and \(n(\theta)\) at \(t=0\) over the full colatitude range, from the per-degree elastic response summed to degree 256. The error is the largest absolute difference divided by the peak of the reference profile. A band of ±1° around the disc edge is excluded from the assertion, since a truncated spectral sum rings at the discontinuity of the load (Gibbs). The error in that band is reported.
Viscoelastic center uplift. \(u(0,t)\) at \(t = 1, 2, 5, 10\) kyr, from the 1-D Maxwell stepper summed over degrees 2–128 with a 20 yr step.

The test does not compare the uplift rate \(\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}t\), the viscoelastic profile away from the center, or the response at \(t = 100\) kyr. The 100 kyr response is left out because the fluid-limit disc sum of the model lies about 2.6 % below the reference, which is within the scatter of the benchmark codes but has not been resolved. The viscoelastic profiles are written to the dump files for inspection.
The reference uses a mixed reference frame: displacement in a center-of-figure-like gauge (\(h_1\approx 0\)) and geoid with \(N_1 = 0\). VILMA2 reproduces it with deg1_frame = "cf", which keeps the solver’s displacement gauge and drops the degree-1 geoid. The default "cm" frame differs from the reference at degree 1 only (see Sea-level equation).

Reference: Martinec et al. (2018), the SLE intercomparison (Martinec et al. 2018), cases A and C2/D3/E2/F1 (SBK reference curves). Tests: test_benchmark_martinec (case A, in make check) and test_benchmark_sle (the four SLE cases, in make check-slow). Asserted: case A within 1.5 % (uplift, horizontal) and 3 % (geoid) of the profile peak; SLE cases within 30 % (uplift), 35 % (horizontal), 12 % (geoid), 8 % (sea surface) and 12 % (relative sea level) of the profile peak. Measured (ifx, albedo): case A 0.5–1.9 %; cases D3, E2 and F1 at most 7.6 %; case C2 up to 28 %, see below.
This benchmark runs the full self-consistent, migrating-coastline sea-level equation driven by the viscoelastic response. It is the benchmark in which VILMA1 took part. It exercises the ocean function, mass conservation, coastline migration, grounded-ice flotation, and the sub-grid sloping coast all together.

title: Benchmark: the sea-level equation
text:
Benchmark structure
The authority for the case definitions is Martinec et al. (2018), Table 4 (not the differing case labels in third-party reimplementations). The paper defines five cases from a small set of building blocks:

Ice (square-root cap \(h(\psi) = h_0\sqrt{(\cos\psi-\cos\alpha)/(1-\cos\alpha)}\), \(\alpha=10°\)): L0 pole/1500 m; L1 colat 25°/lon 75°, 1500 m; L2 same centre, 500 m.
Basin (\(\zeta^{(0)} = b_{\max} - b_0\,e^{-\psi^2/2\sigma^2}\), \(\sigma=26°\)): B0 none; B1 colat 100°/lon 320°, shallow (760/1200); B2 colat 35°/lon 25°, deep (3800/6000, 2200 m at centre).
Time: T0 Heaviside (load held, \(t_f = 10\) kyr); T1 linear growth over 10 kyr then held to 15 kyr.
Ocean: SLE0 none; SLE1 fixed geometry \(O^{(0)}\); SLE2 time-varying (migrating coastline).
Densities \(\rho_{\text{ice}}/\rho_{\text{water}} = 931/1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), \(g_0 = 9.815\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

title: Benchmark: the sea-level equation
text:
Error measure
Every number on this page is a peak-normalized maximum error: the largest absolute difference between model and reference along one profile, divided by the largest absolute value of the reference along that same profile. The two horizontal components are normalized by the peak magnitude of the horizontal vector, since a profile through a symmetry axis nulls one component. This measure is strict in one respect and misleading in another. It reports the single worst point of a profile. It also grows without any change in the absolute error when a profile crosses a region where the field itself is small. Both effects appear in case C2.

section: SLE cases — C2, D3, E2, F1
text:
SLE cases — C2, D3, E2, F1
These cases run the full sea-level equation with the time-varying load at \(\ell_\max = 128\) with a 20 yr step. The reference files give seven columns: longitude or colatitude, vertical displacement, the two horizontal components, the gravitational potential increment, the sea-surface variation, and the SLE result (relative sea level). They are sampled along four profiles per case (figs. 10–13 of the paper). Figs. 10 and 11 pass through the ice cap, along a meridian and a parallel. Figs. 12 and 13 pass through the ocean basin.
Mass is conserved to \(\sim 10^{-16}\) (relative) per step in every case. Three settings control the agreement:

Fixed or migrating ocean. C2 and D3 are fixed-ocean (SLE1) cases. Running them with a migrating coastline drains the basin roughly twice too far, so the fixed-ocean mode (sle_fixed_ocean) must be honored.
Grounded-ice masking. The ice load applies only over grounded ice. Floating ice over the deep basin is carried by the ocean term.
The sub-grid sloping coast (sle_subgrid). The SBK reference uses a sub-grid coast. With a binary coastline the local errors of E2 near the grounding line were 14–42 % during development (not re-measured for this page; test_benchmark_sle.x E2 binary runs that variant). With the sub-grid water-column load they are about 1 %.

What the numbers mean
Cases D3, E2 and F1. The sea surface and relative sea level agree with the reference to within 2 % of the peak in all twelve profiles, which is 0.2–0.8 m in absolute terms. The uplift through the ice cap agrees to about 1 % (0.4–1.0 m of 86–102 m). The percentages of 5–7.6 % belong to fields with a small peak along the profile: the uplift along the basin profiles (0.35–0.5 m of 7–15 m), the horizontal displacement (0.4–0.8 m of 7–15 m) and the geoid (0.02–0.14 m of 0.3–2.7 m). The absolute differences are thus below 1 m everywhere in these three cases.
Case C2. The differences are larger, and the percentages of 21–28 % are not a local effect at the migrating coastline (the ocean of C2 is fixed). Two smooth, large-scale differences explain them. First, the sea surface of the model lies 5.9 m below the reference at every point of all four profiles, which is 4.9 % of the 120 m sea-level fall of this case. Second, the uplift differs from the reference by a smooth pattern of global extent with an amplitude of about 7 m. It is positive on the side of the ice cap and negative on the far side, which is the shape of a degree-1 term. The absolute uplift difference is therefore about the same in all four profiles (7.3–7.8 m). It is 2.5 % of the 309 m peak along the profiles through the ice cap, and 21–23 % of the 34 m peak along the two profiles through the basin. The horizontal differences of 6–7 m behave in the same way. Case C2 has the thickest ice (1500 m, three times that of the other cases) applied as a Heaviside load on a fixed ocean, so a difference in the degree-0 and degree-1 treatment between the two codes is largest here. The same pattern is present in E2 with an amplitude of about 0.3 m. The origin of this difference (reference frame, or the mass budget of the fixed ocean) has not been attributed. The tolerances of the test (30 % and 35 %) are set to pass this case and are therefore not a meaningful bound for the other three.






NoteAn inter-code comparison, not an analytic one



The SBK reference is the output of one code (giapy), not a closed-form solution. Martinec et al. (2018) document a scatter of a few percent between the participating codes. The agreement of D3, E2 and F1 is within that scatter. The uniform offset and the degree-1 pattern of C2 are larger than that and remain open.

title: VILMA2
text:
VILMA2 is a fast, open-source 3D solid-Earth model: a self-gravitating, incompressible, Maxwell-viscoelastic sphere coupled to a self-consistent sea-level equation with migrating coastlines. It is designed as an open-source alternative to VILMA1 inside the CLIMBER-X Earth system model (Willeit et al. 2022), and more generally as a reusable glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) engine for ice-sheet and sea-level work.
The numerical method follows the spectral–finite-element, time-domain approach of Martinec (2000): spherical harmonics horizontally, finite elements radially, and an explicit memory-stress integration of the Maxwell rheology in time. The solver is 3D-ready from the start: laterally varying viscosity uses the same per-degree solve as the 1-D model. It is validated against the published GIA community benchmarks (Spada et al. 2011; Martinec et al. 2018; Weerdesteijn et al. 2023). VILMA2 is free software under the GNU General Public License v3.0.

title: VILMA2
text:
Why this method
The structural advantage of this approach is that, with an explicit Maxwell time scheme, the stiffness solve has no angular coupling. Each spherical-harmonic degree \(\ell\) decouples into an independent, small, banded radial system. This makes the solver embarrassingly parallel and cheap. Lateral (3D) viscosity never couples the harmonics in the solve. It enters only through the explicitly known memory stress, which is evaluated pointwise on the Gauss–Legendre grid and transformed back to spectral space each step (a pseudo-spectral treatment). Its cost lies in these transforms of the memory advance, which dominate the run time of a 3-D run. The 1D and 3D code paths are therefore the same solver.

Status
VILMA2 is validated against the published GIA benchmarks and is starting to be used for science. It is versioned 0.x, so the namelist and the host API may still change. The implemented model comprises the spectral–finite-element solver, the viscoelastic time stepping, the self-consistent sea-level equation with migrating coastlines, rotational feedback, laterally varying (3-D) viscosity, restart and spin-up, online remapping of lon-lat forcing, and a host-coupling API.

What is still open:

Sea-level case C2. A uniform 5.9 m offset in sea surface and a degree-1 pattern of about 7 m in uplift, not yet attributed. The other three cases agree to below 1 m.
The 3-D viscosity path is compared with other codes only in the axisymmetric low-viscosity-zone case (200 yr) and with VILMA1 on the last deglaciation. No multi-code benchmark of a realistic 3-D structure at glacial time scales exists yet.
Toroidal flow driven by lateral viscosity is on by default (l_toroidal = .true.). In the 3-D last deglaciation it changes relative sea level by 2–3 m rms and up to 92 m near the former ice sheets. l_toroidal = .false. makes 3-D runs 1.5–1.8 times faster, for quick runs that do not depend on local sea level (Toroidal flow).
Rotation coupled to the sea-level equation has no published benchmark and is checked for consistency only.
